subsubtopic: CONDUCT OF CANADIAN ARMED FORCES IN GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last I told the hon. member_ for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), in response to a question, that as soon as I had received a report with respect to certain allegations in the German press as
to the conduct of Canadian soldiers in Germany, I would make a statement. I have now received a report and I am glad to say that it does not bear out the lurid statements which have been published.
The Canadian brigade is at present engaged in exercises at Sennelager training area, 50 miles from its base, and two incidents took place in that area recently. The facts of these two incidents as reported to me are as follows:
First, on the night of June 16, a number of Canadian and British soldiers became involved in a brawl in a tavern on the edge of the area and some windows were broken. The arrest of three Canadians by the provost corps followed.
Second, on the night of June 19, a joint Canadian provost corps-German police patrol was searching for a missing motorcycle and in the course of their search entered a tavern near Sennelager just at closing time. Three Canadian soldiers in the tavern refused to leave when requested and were then ordered by the Canadian provost corps to the police car outside. These soldiers called to their friends to help them, which a number of them endeavoured to do, and, in the rough-house which ensued, some uniforms were torn and a Canadian provost lance-corporal suffered a minor cut on the head. Some of the German police, who are always armed, fired their revolvers in the air and the men immediately dispersed. Six soldiers were arrested by the Canadian provost corps and are now awaiting trial.
No German civilians were involved in either incident. The relationship between the Canadian troops and the German population is, and continues to be, friendly and cooperative. This was confirmed, as hon. members may have noted, in Ottawa Tuesday by Dr. Puendor, former burgomaster of Cologne and a member of the Bundestag, who was reported to have said, in relation to these incidents, that Canadian troops are generally considered very friendly and well-behaved, and the newspapers which originated the report are known to be of a sensational variety.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, June 22, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Harris-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act, the Railway Act and the Tariff Board Act to provide for increases in the salaries of the members of the income tax appeal board, the board of transport commissioners and the tariff board.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext: The resolution states in full the purpose of the bill which will follow. The decision to increase the salaries of the members of the various boards follows logically upon the decision to increase the salaries of the judges. It is for the purpose of carrying out a decision which was made consequent upon the other decision.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are few occupations in the world pleasanter than raising people's salaries when a proper case is made for so doing. But at the same time it must be done with a sense of responsibility and that, of course, involves full information.
I think we must also bear in mind the fact that not everybody in Canada at the present time is finding his income going up. There are certain areas where that is anything but the case. I think that consideration puts on us an even greater onus to act with a sense of responsibility.
I therefore wish to ask for full information as to the history of the salaries, what the salaries have been, the last time there was a raise and what the raise is now. I do not
Public Service
think we should too easily assume that these people necessarily are on all fours with each other or that they are necessarily in the same category as the judges. I think various questions enter into the matter. While I certainly am not wishing to oppose the resolution I wish to reserve all rights of consideration until we have full information. The relevant information seems to me to be first of all a brief history of the salary in each case; second, a statement as to the qualifications of those engaged, how long they have been there. Some of them are professional people, I believe, and others not. In general would the minister give us the full information which any responsible person needs to have when considering this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the board of transport commissioners consists of six members. As I think the committee knows, the chairman and deputy chairman are required to be a judge, a retired judge or a barrister of 10 years' standing. At the moment the salary of the chief commissioner is $16,000 and that of the assistant chief commissioner $14,000. The salary is $13,000 for the deputy chief commissioner, and $12,000 for the other three commissioners. It is proposed to increase the salaries as follows: The chief commissioner, $18,500. I should add that is automatic upon the Judges Act being assented to because the statute provides that he will be paid the same salary as the president of the exchequer court. The assistant chief commissioner will receive $15,500, the deputy chief commissioner, $14,500 and the other commissioners, $13,500. It will be seen that only the chief commissioner has his salary increased by the amount of the increase given to judges. The other increases are $1,500 each.
As to the income tax appeal board, in this case there are certain qualifications required by statute as far as the chairman and the assistant chairman are concerned. At the present time the chairman receives $14,400, the assistant chairman $13,000 and the other two members $11,000. It will be seen that the salary of the chairman is that of a judge of the exchequer court. He is being increased to $16,900, which will be the salary of a judge of the exchequer court under the amendment to the Judges Act.

These qualifications are of course held by those now in these offices. In the case of the board of transport commissioners, as my hon. friend said a while ago, some of the members are civil servants of long standing and many years' service in the public service. In the case of the income tax appeal board the member most recently appointed is the assistant chairman who has had something like two years' service. The other members have been there for some time. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext:
This resolution, Mr. Chairman, makes me feel that I should start off by saying, "here we go again". Perhaps I should say that whether or not the government is thoroughly familiar with scripture, at least those across the way seem to be familiar with the verse that says that to him that hath shall be given. Here again we have increases in salaries proposed for people who, I admit, are in very responsible positions but nevertheless whose salaries are already at a level which most Canadians would consider to be more than adequate. I know how unpopular it is for me to make these repeated references to the failure of the government to do something about the position of those of our people who are in the lower brackets, with respect to income tax exemptions, with respect to the position of old age pensioners and other groups.
fMr. Harris.]
As I said at the start, "here we go again". We cannot seem to get action from the government on behalf of the people in this country who are really in need. Yet, it seems very easy for the government to bring in resolution after resolution, bill after bill, increasing salaries in cases where the levels are already reasonably adequate or, in the view of many Canadians, more than adequate.
I wish to point out also, Mr. Chairman, that in the case of all of these positions but one, that is in the case of all those on the board of transport commissioners; in the case of all those who are members of the income tax appeal board and in the case of all those who are members of the tariff board except the chairman, there have been increases during the last four years. As a matter of fact, in the case of the income tax appeal board there were substantial increases two years ago. In the case of the tariff board, there were substantial increases to all except the chairman two years ago. In the case of the board of transport commissioners, there were substantial increases to all the members four years ago. In the meantime it is many years since some people in this country, whose case we plead, have had any improvement in their position. I suggest a better perspective should be taken of matters of this kind.
The minister said that these increases follow logically upon the increases granted by this house to the judges. Well, if that is the case it follows logically that we feel as we did about those increases, that before they are granted increases should be provided for some of those in this country, our old age pensioners and others, who really need increases. When I made this reference yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton suggested that these things should be treated separately on their own merits. That is a good argument; it is very plausible. The only trouble is that in the case of those who already have sufficient, their case gets considered on its alleged merits but the case of these other groups is delayed and delayed.
Like the hon. member for Greenwood, I recognize it is a very pleasant position for the Minister of Finance to be in to be raising salaries. It is a pleasant position for anyone to be improving the lot or the security of any of our fellow citizens. But I ask for a little perspective, I ask for concern for those of our Canadian citizens who really need consideration rather than this constant stream of increases for those who are already up in the income brackets enjoyed by less than 1 per cent of the people of this country.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, briefly I should like to indicate that we should exercise a

little caution when considering this resolution, and perhaps should have more information. The mere fact that the resolution follows an increase in the salaries of judges, and the fact that that subject was given considerable thought yesterday, would not justify our rushing it through. Nor would the fact that it is offered late in the session give us cause to hurry.
I have had an opportunity only to look into the increases in salary for the board of transport commissioners, and some thoughts come to my mind in this connection. First of all let me say that I believe the board of transport commissioners is doing a good job, and that we have good men on that board. They seem to be discharging very well the important duties placed before them. I had a personal experience before the board this summer when they were considering the discontinuing of a railway line in the maritime provinces, and I felt that, while their judgment may not have appealed to me in that instance, they did look carefully into the matter, and operated in a fair and judicial manner. Even though nowadays they may be performing their duties better than they were performed at some other times I do feel we should be most careful that we do not apply exactly the same reasoning in their case as we did in connection with the judges.
It is true that the salary of the chief commissioner is fixed in that it is joined to that of the president of the exchequer court. Nevertheless, when one looks back to the increases that have occurred since 1947 in the salaries of the chief commissioner, the deputy, the assistant chief and others, he must see some inconsistencies in those increases. For example the increases have not been exactly the same in all four instances. The salary of the assistant chief and the other commissioners remained the same on two occasions, following which they were jumped to a point where they occupied the same relative position. I admit they are in that position today.
I should like to know if these increases are justified, and if they are computed on exactly the same basis as those for the judges. For example it was pointed out that the judges should have salary increases because the bench required strengthening. It is true that the Turgeon report said the board of transport commissioners should be strengthened. But has it not now been strengthened, and should there be further increases?
At this resolution stage I would leave the thought that the members of this party have shown consistency in being wary of increases. While we did support the increases in judges' salaries, definite reasons for those increases 50433-327
Public Service
were advanced when it was pointed out that good men had indicated they did not wish to go on the bench because of the lower salaries paid. And we also took note of the fact that there seemed to be some agreement that the bench in some respect was weak.
I do not know if the same reasons apply in the present case. I understand that in 1946 the Gordon report recommended that the board of transport commissioners should have an increase of about $2,000 over the salaries received by the members of other permanent boards in a comparable position. I should like to know if that principle is being maintained. I would also reiterate the fears expressed by the previous speaker when he said that the approach to this whole matter does not seem to be as it should be. Are these across the board increases, or are they given because there will be a discrepancy in the salaries of the other members with the chief commissioner automatically receiving the increase being granted to judges?
I view the whole measure with some apprehension and I should like to be given more definite reasons why these increases should be made at this time.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said most of the things I would have said had I spoken earlier. All I can say now is that I agree with everything he has said. I noted his reference to the scriptures, and possibly as a layman I may be allowed to draw attention to the other half of the quotation he referred to. The hon. member said the government was at least fulfilling the scriptures in giving to those who already had, but by the same token we are fulfilling the other half of that quotation by taking away from those who have not even that which they hath. Every time we increase wages or salaries we add to the spiral of inflation. If we are not taking care of those at the bottom as well as those at the top then we are taking away the little which those at the bottom have. I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce is taking note of my remarks and will look into this matter of fulfilling the scriptures and have a word with the Minister of Finance.

hon. member has been referring to the scriptures and I wonder if it would be out of the way if I asked him to turn up Micah 6, verse 8, which I think will provide an answer to all these questions.

What I said yesterday
applies also to the resolution now before us. I do not know whether the members of the government have noticed, but for some time

Public Service
the press of this country has been drawing attention to the fact that possibly the wage structure has gone up high enough. As a matter of fact employers are increasing their resistance to requests for increases in wages, and at times are even proposing reductions in wages.
When the government proposes to increase the salaries of people who are already receiving very substantial salaries I see no reason in the world why trade unions should withhold their hands in any way. They should go out after everything they can get because we are setting an example here.
I remember last year the chairman of the board of transport commissioners criticized the railway employees for seeking higher wages. Following that I put some questions on the order paper as to the salary of the chairman and the salaries of the members of the board of transport commissioners. I found that those salaries were quite substantial then, and we are now going to add to them.
As I said yesterday, we are building up a top-heavy society by adding to the wealth of the few at the top and taking away from those at the bottom. Every society which has been built on that basis has destroyed itself and the same thing will happen to ours unless we mend our ways. There is no reason in the world for these increases. People who today are getting over $10,000 or $12,000 a year have a very good living, particularly when their years of retirement are provided for with an adequate pension.
I do not suppose anything I say will have any effect; I suppose the government will go on and look after those who are already looked after and fail to look after the old age pensioners and those who retired from our railways, the civil service and other employments on very low pensions. I do not believe that hon. members of this house have any understanding of the struggle which so many people in this rich country have to go through day after day trying to make ends meet on inadequate incomes.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that salaries, wages and dividends are going up year after year, with the exception of the income of the farmer which has been going down year after year. The main burden of these increases will fall upon our farm population.
The point I am particularly interested in in trying to decide whether or not these increases are justified is the yardstick used by the government in coming to a decision of this kind. It is very hard for us to decide whether there is any justification for increases of this type. There must be some yardstick
fMr. Maclnnis.]
used by the government and I wonder if the minister would tell us what that is.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES

Mr. Chairman, when the Minister of Finance opened the debate this morning he made a remark which I think pinpoints the whole problem we are facing. He said that these increases follow logically on the increases in judges' salaries. I should like to have a little further clarification from the minister on that point. I should like to know just how he justifies a statement of that kind and I propose to make a few comments before the minister replies. In doing so I shall refer only to the salaries of the members of the board of transport commissioners.
Before I go on to do that may I point out that if the policy of the government is that increases follow logically then I am afraid there will be no end to it; these increases will go right down the line.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT, RAILWAY ACT, TARIFF BOARD ACT  AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES
speechtext:
He is very well taken care of under the Railway Act because he automatically gets the salary of the president of

the exchequer court. When the salary of the president of that court goes up, pursuant to the bill which received third reading early this morning, the salary of the chairman of the board of transport commissioners will go up to the same amount. Furthermore, section 10 of the Railway Act provides that the chief commissioner, should he not be reappointed at the end of the 10-year period, automatically becomes a judge of the exchequer court. There is no discretion given in the act; he automatically becomes a judge of the exchequer court. In these ways there is some connection between his salary and the judges' salaries, because he automatically gets one of the highest salaries paid to any judge in the country.
When the minister goes further and says the increased salaries payable to the other members of the board follow logically on the increases under the judges' salaries act, I see no strength whatever in that argument. I think the assistant chief commissioner is a lawyer or an advocate by training. I do not know whether or not any of the others are, but certainly some of them are not. I think their salaries should be dealt with on the merits, and not come in as an appendix to a bill which increases the salaries of the judges.

I now touch on our export markets. Canada has rich fisheries on both our coasts. We have a comparatively small population and we are very poor fish eaters, which means that exports of fish are very important to the industry. Here again I am very happy to report a substantial increase in exports last year, up 17 per cent over 1953 from $114 million to $133 million. I am also happy to report increased diversification of these exports. The United States is still our biggest and best market. We have no currency problem there of course. They are a great market and prices are good. That is true, I suppose, of most products as far as the American market is concerned.
There is another aspect of fisheries, however, which makes the American market especially important to us. Fish is a very highly perishable product and so, of course, the best markets are the ones closest to the source of supply. The United States share of our exports declined from 72-7 per cent to 67-8 per cent, and the shares of other countries increased accordingly. I think that is a healthy sign because we do not want to have all our fish in one basket. United Kingdom exports doubled from $5-2 million to $12 million. Canned salmon is worthy of special note because, there, overseas sales increased from $14-6 million to $24 million. This increase is due to the industry's buy British program, an aggressive sales policy,

The $90 million of fish which we export to the United States is, of course, of very great importance to the fishing industry. It is two-thirds of our exports, and our exports in all are about 75 per cent of our fisheries production. I should like to pay tribute here to the very close co-operation which exists between the two fisheries associations of Canada and the United States, the fisheries council of Canada and the national fisheries institute of America. These associations are composed of all producers and wholesalers, the people who handle fish in both countries, and through their committees they have been able to work out very close co-operation in such things as quality, standards and types of packages. The federal government and the United States department of fish and wildlife have of course
assisted in this development. It is very interesting to see the increased American participation in the Canadian fisheries council through ownership of plants up here and the greatly increased Canadian participation in the American institute because of our interest in their market.
I should now like to make the announcement to which I referred with regard to salt cod. There are some 15,000 fishermen in Newfoundland, Quebec and the maritime provinces who are dependent on the production and sale of various types of salted fish, cod, haddock, pollock, hake and cusk, for the major share of their incomes from fishing. These fishermen are generally in the lowest income group in the fisheries, their products being sold in the low price markets of the Caribbean and southern Europe.

Because of this condition, these fishermen have at times asked for assistance under the Fisheries Prices Support Act.
The Fisheries Prices Support Act was never intended to supplement general low prices on world markets. It was intended to compensate for sudden drops in market prices which seriously affected fishermen's returns, and to assist by purchasing fish for which no markets were available. The act has been used for both these purposes in the past. I will submit the record of assistance since the passage of the act if requested to do so when item 153 is under consideration.
In 1953 there was a decline in the world price of salt cod, and price support of $1.12 a quintal, 112 pounds of dried fish, was paid on Newfoundland shore-cured fish. No price support was paid on the fish produced on the mainland. This year the Newfoundland fishermen's organizations applied for price support on the 1954 production. The price received by the fishermen was a little higher than the 1953 price without price support. For one of the commonest grades, Madeira, they got $10.05 this year against $9.85 last year on the market. The 1954 catch was 20 per cent greater than the 1953 catch, however, so fishermen's income in 1954 was greater without price support than it was on 1953's smaller catch with price support.
No real problem exists in marketing the 1954 fish and no unsold surplus of any consequence is anticipated. The mainland fishermen and producers, those in the three maritime provinces and in Quebec, fish in the same general area and their fish is sold competitively in the same markets. They have not applied for price support and feel that if price support is paid to the Newfoundland fishermen it will mean unfair competition by way of a government bonus to their competitors.
A further complication is the close integration of the fresh and frozen fish trade with the salt fish trade, many fishermen producing for both markets. Any suggestion of price support or subsidies on fish exported to the United States would immediately raise a cry for countervailing duties on our fish. They have the sort of legislation we discussed here the other evening for putting extra duties on any product which is subsidized for export in the country of origin. As I have pointed out, the United States is very much our largest customer for fish of all sorts. Therefore it has been decided not to pay price support on the 1954 production of Newfoundland salt cod.
It is, however, appreciated that the salt cod industry does need assistance in the
Supply-Fisheries
present transitional period. Such assistance, however, should be extended to the whole Atlantic salt cod industry and not just to the industry in one province. Undoubtedly the best way is to assist in the most important outside ingredient in the production of salt cod, namely, salt. These fishermen have tremendous resources of fish available to them, but the only way they have of preserving these fish in many areas is to salt them for the market. The cost of the salt in the more remote areas in relation to the price of the finished product has forced many fishermen to leave the industry. A rebate on salt has been suggested as a temporary measure until the department's industrial development program to modernize these fisheries reaches these fishing areas.
The government is therefore proposing to proceed with an arrangement to pay a rebate to fishermen and others at the rate of 50 per cent of the cost of the salt delivered to the point of production in the calendar year 1955. The payment will be based on the proof of purchase and the proof of the use of such salt in the production of designated fisheries products. The designated product will include salt cod, haddock, pollock, hake and cusk. The fishermen this year will, for this purpose, not have to take any action now other than to be sure to save their records of salt purchases and sales of salted fish. Detailed instructions will be made available as soon as possible. Fishermen will submit only one claim application form which will be provided at the end of the production year. These forms will be available in September.
During the coming year careful study will be made to see whether the present methods of purchasing, packaging and distributing salt can be improved so as to further reduce the cost for the fishermen. The co-operation of the provinces in this matter will be welcome. On the basis of this study, recommendations will be made for a continuation or a change in this assistance in future years. Computed on the basis of estimates currently available, the over-all assistance at 50 per cent rebate would be as follows: Newfoundland, the number of fishermen engaged in salt fishing there is 9,000, the rebate will total $375,000 or about $42 per fisherman; in Nova Scotia, 2,500 fishermen and a rebate of $80,000 will work out at about $32 per fisherman; New Brunswick, about 1,000 fishermen in the salt cod industry and a rebate of $22,500 works out at $22 per fisherman; Prince Edward Island, 500 fishermen and a $3,500 rebate works out to $7 per fisherman; Quebec, the Saguenay and Gaspe shores, 1,500 fishermen and a $19,000 rebate works out at $13 per fisherman. The total number of fishermen affected will be around 15,000 and

Supply-Fisheries
the total cost to the government in the current year will be about half a million dollars. As no funds for this purpose are available in the present estimates, the Minister of Finance will present a supplementary estimate for the approval of parliament.
Now, proceeding with the report of the main activities of the department, I come to our program of fisheries management and development which is of course primarily dependent on fisheries research. I will discuss the general activities of the fisheries research board on the item for that board, but I might say that they have made satisfactory progress on many fronts. One of the many interesting problems they are now studying is the matter of the utilization of dogfish. We have countless numbers of dogfish on both coasts. They give our fishermen considerable trouble. During wartime their livers were a very valuable source of vitamins and a good industry was built on both coasts on fishing dogfish for their livers. The development of synthetic vitamins after the war, of course, ruined that market. Great use is made in England of dogfish.
The English, of course, eat about three times as much fish as we do. Over half of that fish is consumed through the fish and chips shops, the equivalent of our hamburger and hot dog stands. At least half of the fish used in fish and chips shops is dogfish. We, in this country, have never made much use of it. We have conducted experiments on trying to make fishmeal out of dogfish. One of the difficulties is the high ammonia content of the flesh. However, experiments have gone far enough ahead now for one of our commercial companies on the coast to put in a pilot plant this year, and they will see whether or not economic use can be made of dogfish. It will be a great boon to the fishermen in two ways. First of all it will reduce the great number of dogfish which prey on other fish in the sea, and it will also provide another source of income for the fishermen.
The other interesting thing is the steady expansion of our scientific work in the field of oceanography. Fisheries scientists have always realized that one of the secrets of the movement of fish is linked with the great tidal and seasonal movements of the oceans of the world. Both our research stations at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and Nanaimo in British Columbia, have oceanographers who are pursuing this work. The navy, and the hydrographic section of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, have assisted us in this work because these studies are very important to them, too.
We have had a very interesting example of how practical even such an abstract study 
as oceanography can be. The British Columbia electric railway company laid the first under-water high tension power line from the mainland to Vancouver island. The engineers of this company came to our department to ask for the services of our oceanographers in charting the best route for the cables and to give them data on water levels, tides and salinity. This company paid for the use of these people, but they were so pleased with the results that they have voluntarily made a gift of $5,000 to the institute of oceanography at the University of British Columbia as a tribute to the work of our men in his field.
We help our fishermen in a more direct way so far as locating fish is concerned. This is done in two ways, that is, exploratory fishing, finding new fishing grounds, and demonstration fishing or trying out new gears, new inventions and perfecting them before recommending them to the fishermen. Fishermen have always been low income workers generally, and therefore cannot afford to venture very far away from the grounds where they know from past experience the fish are going to be found, nor can they venture large sums in new capital equipment unless they are pretty sure that capital equipment is going to work. One of the functions of our department is to do both exploratory fishing and demonstration fishing. On the west coast most of the exploratory fishing has been done by the industry itself because that is the most prosperous and most advanced section of our fishing industry. However, we have done considerable exploratory fishing out there for shrimp. Shrimp are in very great demand in North America, and are one of the few fish we do not obtain in sufficient quantities to supply the Canadian demand. We have to import them from the United States. We have encouraged commercial fishermen to fish these new grounds, both by trap and by trawl, and are very happy to report a substantial increase in the production of shrimp as a consequence.
On the east coast we have now finished a complete mapping of the great cod banks, the fishing grounds surrounding Newfoundland. Some of these banks have now been fished for almost 500 years, so you would think they were all well known. The fact remains that many of the inshore grounds have not been developed. We did this by a combination of engaging experienced fishermen and their vessels to do regular patrol explorations under the direction of our scientists and by the use of our own vessels. One of the most significant developments has been

the finding of excellent grounds near Bona-vista, the riding represented by my colleague the acting minister of fisheries, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Today there are 15 longliners based on Bonavista which are fishing these grounds discovered by our exploratory fishing. We have also done a great deal of tagging of codfish along the shores of Newfoundland to get more information on the actual migration of the fish from year to year.
In the maritime area our most significant exploratory fishing has been for scallops. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has in his riding the great fishing town of Digby which until recent years was the source of most of the scallops used in Canada. There is a good market for scallops so we did exploratory fishing in the banks, out in the gulf and in the ocean and discovered excellent grounds on the St. Pierre bank and Brown's bank. As a result of that, in the last four years the production of scallops in Canada has trebled from half a million pounds a year to a million and a half pounds a year. First discoveries had an unfortunate effect on the market, so far as my hon. friend's fishermen are concerned, because the increased production dropped the price; but the price is now back at a reasonable level.
We have also done a lot of work on trying to devise more effective drags for scallop fisheries, and here we had the co-operation of the navy, which lent us deep-sea divers to watch the underground operations of these draggers as they scraped the sea bottom for scallops, to note the effectiveness of the gear and what damage was done to the beds, and what immature scallops were left.
We are continuing discoveries in a field of research in what is commonly called the great herring mystery in the gulf of St. Lawrence. We have a large and successful herring industry on the west coast. Our scientists have done a remarkable job there in forecasting the size of the runs and the time of year in which they will appear, and the quotas which should be established, to assure that we are going to have perpetual fisheries.
There is a very fine herring and sardine fishery of course in the bay of Fundy, mainly in that area represented by the hon. member for Charlotte. But in the gulf area itself there is a tremendous stock of herring which is very hard to locate. There have been very large catches, and then years will go by with very small catches. This spring a disease hit these herring, and the large herring population was shown by the very great numbers of dead herring washed up on the beaches, and scraped up by trawlers fishing for cod
Supply-Fisheries
and for haddock. We have had extensive research done there. We are not yet able to predict with any accuracy, as we are on the west coast, where these runs will occur. However, our research was far enough advanced that this year an English fishing firm from Lowestoft, England, a firm experienced in herring fishing, has come to Nova Scotia, and with the assistance of the provincial government has launched a fishery for herring in the gulf, using the drift net method of the North sea.
Thus far they have had quite good catches, and we hope through their experience, plus our research, we will solve the problem and establish the east coast herring fisheries on a basis as regular and as lucrative as the herring fisheries of the west coast.
So far as demonstration fishing is concerned,
I think our-

Before the minister proceeds to discuss demonstration fishing, I take it the company was fishing in the north part of Nova Scotia. I believe they have come down to what we call the southwest part of Nova Scotia, and have left the north or the Northumberland strait and the gulf of St. Lawrence, down to what we call the southwest, on the Atlantic ocean.

The reason this took place is quite clear. They thought herring were more likely present in the southwest. It is because this company has had experience in herring fishing. They are conducting large-scale exploratory fishing, on a commercial scale.
Keturning to the subject of demonstration fishing, one of the most interesting things we have done in the last year is in connection with dories. In the days of the old fishing schooners, such as the Bluenose, there was a tremendous fleet of schooners fishing the Grand Banks, and those schooners were loaded with dories-one-man or two-man dories. Those are the small rowboats which were put over the side each morning from which the fishermen operated, both with long lines, along the bottom, and with hand lines.
But, over the years, it was found more and more difficult to get fishermen to fish in dories. Perhaps this was the most dangerous phase of fishing, where men in these small rowboats would be a hundred miles at sea, out on the Grand Banks where the waters of the gulf stream meet the waters of Davis strait, an area of storm and fog.
And as conditions improved in the fishing industry it was found that fewer and fewer men would go dory fishing. As a matter of fact the only fleet on the Grand Banks using dories today are the 62 Portuguese ships,

which usually carry 75 one-man dories. We have a good fleet of bankers which were not being used because of the lack of men for these small dories. So our experimental station devised a larger powered dory. The other dories, of course, relied on the use of oars. The power does two things. It makes the boat safer and gives greater mobility, and also provides mechanical power for the lifting of long lines quickly and safely. Four of these dories can be carried on one banker.
Our experiments thus far have been quite successful, in fishing, but trouble has been encountered launching the heavier dories in rough water. The single-man dory was much easier to launch. The results have been very encouraging, however, and we are proceeding with this project.
On the west coast a group of fishermen in 1950 began to work on a mid-water trawl. In Canada most of our fishing is done close to the surface with lures, with gill nets or with seines, or right on the bottom with trawlers scraping the bottom. With modern electronic recording devices and echo-sounders it is easy to locate the fish at various levels between the bottom and the top. So a lot of work has been done to devise a satisfactory mid-water trawl which can be fished at every level fish are found. Fishermen on the west coast started work on this, themselves. By 1953 they had encountered many obstacles, and had asked for help from our west coast experimental station. The work thus far has been very successful. These trawls are making catches of between 10 and 30 tons per drag; and we are looking forward to quite a development in such gear, once it has been fully perfected.
One other step forward has been the development on the west coast of the use of refrigerated sea water for holding fish in fishing boats and fish tanks. Today the common procedure is to put fish in the hold, spread ice, then more fish on top of that. The result is that the fish in the bottom become badly bruised from the pressure of the other fish on top. A ship also has to carry sufficient ice on the outward journey to do for the whole trip. Our engineers on the west coast have rigged up ships with cooling systems which use sea water, cooling down that sea water and using it for refrigeration with the result that the fish are no longer crushed. They are suspended in water and arrive in first-class condition. More and more of our packers are using the refrigerated sea water device, which was invented by our department.
On both coasts the modernization of our fleets is going ahead steadily. This is seen mostly in mechanization. On the west coast 
gill nets are put out and taken in on drums, rather than putting out the gill nets by hand. In the last two or three years our big seiners have found similar but larger drums effective in laying their heavy seines. This has resulted in a situation where, instead of having crews of six or seven, the ships carry crews of three or four.
Nylon nets are now being used everywhere on the west coast and their use is increasing on the east coast. The government's part on the east coast in the improvement of the fleet is done mostly through subsidies we pay to the classes of draggers and long-liners, designed mainly by our naval architects, and put in service on the east coast. We pay a subsidy of $165 a ton to fishermen who construct these improved types of boats. So far we have encouraged the construction of 77 draggers and 125 longliners, and paid a total subsidy of about $800,000.
We have a very effective engineering branch in our department, which has tried to show the world that in this country we can have fish and power, and fish and industry. There is a sorry tale in most countries, that when industry or power entered the scene, fishing operations declined. That is one reason why more and more of the older countries send their fleets so many thousands of miles to other grounds.
In this country we have fisheries under federal control. The Fisheries Act does give us power to insist that before any obstruction, such as a power dam, is placed in a stream, provision must be made for the passage of the fish using that stream. The same is true in connection with pollution by industry. We have power to insist that proper steps be taken so that the effluent from industrial plants shall not poison a stream.
We have a most imposing list of engineering accomplishments in this field, including the building of fishways around dams, and the building of fishways around falls to ensure that salmon especially shall have the easiest possible access to the spawning grounds. And we have a good record, too, in connection with the prevention of industrial pollutions. We try to look to the future to see the trend of industrial development before it actually starts because that is the easiest way to assure necessary fishery precautions. For example, last year we had an engineer and a biologist up in northern British Columbia and the Yukon to look at this great, new Frobisher development, which will start up there in the next two or three years, to see what the effect will be then on the fish population up there. The fish population is not too important commercially but it is of great importance to the Indians

and other residents there. I can discuss this in more detail on the item covering our engineering services.
One of the most vexing matters in connection with fisheries is the question of territorial waters. Countries which have rich fisheries off their coasts naturally want those fisheries kept for the use of their own nationals, while other countries which have no fisheries or which have exhausted their fisheries want the right to fish in such waters. The historic three-mile limit has no relation at all to fisheries. That was the distance the old-fashioned cannon could fire so ships kept further out than that. Fisheries conservationists around the world are agreed that it is impossible to have an adequate conservation policy if it is going to be limited to a three-mile strip and if other nations can come up to that boundary and exploit without any rules or regulations the fish which the country having the coasts has maintained.
This matter has been before the United Nations for some years and a special committee was struck to discuss it. Each country concerned is making a report. Our committee has been working now for two years, headed by Dean Curtis of the law school of the University of British Columbia. Its report has been submitted to the minister of external affairs who mentioned it at a recent meeting of the committee on external affairs. The whole problem will be discussed at the 1956 meeting of the general assembly.
This spring in Rome a conference was held of 55 fishing nations of the world to discuss the whole problem of the conservation of the living resources of the sea. The meeting was told specifically not to discuss this matter of territorial waters, but that number of nations simply could not get going without discussing what is a most difficult problem. The nations were divided almost equally between what are called the coastal states, those nations such as our own which have rich fisheries on their coasts and which naturally want their control extended, and freedom of the seas states, countries which have no fisheries on their own shores and who are anxious to come in and fish other waters on the historic right of freedom of the seas.
The matter has been brought very much to a head by the action last year of three South American countries in arbitrarily extending their boundaries 200 miles out to sea and picking up and arresting whaling ships and United States tuna clippers which were fishing in that area. There is no question that the fishermen of our country would welcome such a declaration here in
Supply-Fisheries
Canada. Hon. members from the maritimes will recall that a 200-mile extension off Newfoundland would include all the Grand Banks areas which have been fished now for 500 years by one nation. This summer in St. John's the Portuguese celebrated the 500th year that they have fished the Grand Banks. This nation claims that they had established historic rights to these high-seas fisheries long before there was a Canada.
However, we have not waited for a decision on this matter. We have tried another approach to conservation by international agreements on the high seas and today Canada is almost ringed with these most excellent international commissions which do a wonderful job in bringing about intelligent international co-operation and control to assure that there is going to be enough fish for all the nations fishing there. Our commissions have done such an outstanding job, this past year especially, that I think I should say a word on each of them when the particular item comes up.
However, there are two of our fisheries which are not covered. The first and most important is the pink salmon fishery on the west coast. We have five kinds of salmon on the west coast, six really if you consider the red spring salmon and the white spring salmon as being different species. The most important is the sockeye salmon, a four-year fish. The two least valuable have always been regarded as the pink salmon, a small two-year fish, and the chum salmon. In 1930 a fisherman was lucky if he got two cents for the whole of a pink salmon, but under this year's agreement he is going to get 8f cents a pound for pink salmon and the value of the Fraser river run will be about $4 million.
While we have had since 1937 an international salmon agreement to control and develop the sockeye salmon resources on the Fraser and to divide the catch equally between the United States and ourselves we have no such commission for the pink salmon. We Canadians have always got a much smaller proportion of the pink catch, mainly because the Americans were in a much better position to catch these salmon. They come in from the open Pacific, sweep down the south tip of Vancouver island, and then pass through United States waters before coming up past the mouth of the Fraser and entering the Fraser.
For years we have asked for a pink salmon commission similar to the sockeye salmon commission, but there has been a certain reluctance on the part of the United States fishing industry to have such a treaty because they were getting 80 per cent of the catch while we were getting only 20 per cent. In

Supply-Fisheries
recent years our fleet has stepped up its catch and has now reached the position for the first time where it is getting almost 40 per cent of the catch.
I have encouraged our fishermen to make an all-out assault on this fishery this year. Two years ago in order to encourage deep-sea fishing we permitted the entry of 15 large deep-sea seiners from the United States and as an encouragement promised the Canadians who brought them in that half the duty would be remitted at the end of the first year's deep-sea fishing and the other half at the end of the second year's deep-sea fishing. I am quite sure that with these boats and with our own seiner fleet operating in outside waters this year our fishermen, catching the fish before they enter United States waters, will be able to pass the United States share of the catch. I hope the United States will then be more amenable to having a conservation treaty similar to the sockeye treaty, than to continuing a policy of each nation trying to out-fish the other.
Our fishermen are certainly convinced of the need of a pink salmon treaty and at last the United States fishermen are also convinced. The unions in the state of Washington and the province of British Columbia had a joint meeting this spring which was attended I believe by the hon. member for New Westminster. At that meeting they both endorsed the idea of such a treaty. Once again I have asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to officially raise this matter with the United States.
Our fishermen do not care so much whether the new treaty is under the international North Pacific commission or is attached to the present international sockeye salmon commission. On the whole they would prefer the salmon commission because .of the excellent work that commission has done in rehabilitating the Fraser run.
The one other fishery which is not specifically covered by an international commission is our seal fishery. Of course seals are animals, but sealing and whaling are generally referred to as fisheries. For many years we had an item in the estimates dealing with the Pribilof fur seals. This was purely a revenue item and it has been removed from the estimates and put under the financial administration vote. At one time there were great resources of Pacific fur seal but ruthless hunting by ships of many nations on the high seas reduced the herd to about 150,000. Canada, the United States, Japan and Russia entered into a conservation treaty which was later abandoned by Russia and

Japan. But as a result of conservation under this treaty there are now somewhere between two and three million seals. The killing is done on a share basis, and we get 20 per cent of the catch. This year the government of Canada grossed $1,002,221 from the sale of 12,776 skins.
We now have a problem created by too great an increase in the number of fur seals. The fishermen of all four nations fishing the north Pacific say that they are doing too much damage to their fisheries. Our scientists calculate that the fur seal herd eats twice as much fish in one week as all Canada eats in one year. This fall the four nations are having a meeting to review the whole problem and a scientific study is being made to see whether the rate of killing should not be increased to decrease the size of the herd. On the east coast we have another great herd of harp seals which come down each spring from Davis strait and whelp off the coast of Newfoundland and in the gulf of St. Lawrence. Last year there were only four vessels that went out sealing from Newfoundland. Three of them were lost in the ice. There was, fortunately, no loss of crews. A century ago there were 400 vessels out of Newfoundland engaged in this industry. This year we had 12 vessels out of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, and none were lost. They killed 140,000 seals, and about 60,000 seals were killed by landsmen, men operating from shore in Labrador, Newfoundland and Quebec. The total value was about $150,000. At the same time there was a Norwegian fleet operating off Labrador, and their kill amounted to about $230,000. That kill is close to the limit which our scientists say this herd will support. We have not an international treaty, but we have an understanding with Norway on the opening date of the season.
I normally would not mention this except that this spring there was considerable publicity given to protests against the inhumanity of seal hunting. I received a great number of letters from the humane societies across the country and from individual people asking whether it was true and what could be done about it. This sealing is probably the most dangerous and ill-rewarding occupation in all the fishing industry. The seals killed are of two types. One is the small white coat, a baby seal less than 30 days old, and the other, adult seal about a year. The white coat is killed by a hard blow with a club at the back of the neck, in the same way as the three-year-old seals are killed on Pribilof island. The adult seals are killed with high powered rifles. Any killing, whether it is in the slaughter house, by the hangman or the killing of seals, is brutal. We aim, of course.

to have brutality cut down to as little as possible. I think that the report originated mainly in the fact that when the baby seals are killed they are skinned immediately. Apparently the observer noted that the carcasses were still quivering after they were skinned and thought the little seals were skinned alive. Our scientists state, and farmers will understand this, that it is the same as when a chicken has its head cut off. Though the chicken is dead it will still run around the farm lot, because its nervous system is still in operation. We try to watch this killing as closely as possible. The minister of provincial affairs in Newfoundland called a committee meeting in Newfoundland to discuss the matter. He is also head of the humane society in Newfoundland. We have agreed that this coming season we will watch this matter very closely.
One of the last things I should like to mention is the matter of fishermen's education. We have in our estimates, and have had for some years, a vote to assist in co-operative education at the St. Francis Xavier University in Nova Scotia, Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere in Quebec and the University of British Columbia in British Columbia. They have done a good job in teaching the fishermen to help themselves and in organizing the credit union movement about which so much has been said favourably in the banking and commerce committee in recent days.
We have, however, given more help than that. Our research board is carrying on certain projects with the universities. We have given them $20,000 to carry out certain research with their graduate students which we would otherwise carry out in our laboratories. We have a new vote of $25,000 for scholarships. We are having difficulty in recruiting the type of scientists we would like for our fisheries research board. Today when a young man graduates in physiology, zoology or biology, there are so many openings for him to go into industrial science where the pay is high that it is becoming more and more difficult to recruit the type of scientists we want for the fisheries research board. Many scholarships are open to graduate students in other fields but few in fisheries. This year we are offering through the national research council graduate scholarships to students who are proposing to go into the fishing industry as a career to enable them to get assistance in their graduate years. This is confined to graduate students. We shall also guarantee them work in summers as student assistants, and in the end work with our research board.
One other thing we have done, which I think is a significant step forward. We have

no fishermen's school in Canada. The way a boy learns to be a fisherman in Canada is by going to sea with his father and watching him fish. Fishing used to be a rather primitive matter, on a boat with sails and a simple net; but with modern mechanization of fishing and the long range of our boats, better education is needed today. Most of the great fishing nations of the world such as Portugal, Norway, Britain and Russia have very good fishing schools. This spring, as an experiment, we started at the University of British Columbia a school for professional fishermen, not for boys. The course was devised by the fisheries department, the university extension department, the fishing companies, the fishermen's union, the native brotherhood, which is the Indian union of fishermen, and the fishermen's co-operative organization. The course of studies is an excellent one and it is well worth while putting it on the record, because I am sure there will be requests from other parts for similar courses:
Oceanography, by our scientists who study oceanography.
Conservation of each of our major fisheries, by the experts from our research board..
The use of gears, ropes and fibres, by a man experienced in the field.
Mid-water trawl, by a scientist working on that subject.
Maintaining quality of fish, by our inspectors.
Navigation, by the head of the navigation school in Vancouver.
Engines, by representatives from the major engine companies.
Electronics-and a modern fishing boat is almost like an aeroplane in the number of electronic devices it has in its wheelhouse- by representatives of the various electronic companies.
First aid by the St. John Ambulance Association.
Search and rescue, our form of coastguard, by the air force officer who heads that branch.
International law as applied to fisheries, by the dean of the law school at the University of British Columbia.
Off-season employment, by the head of the selective service.
Meteorology, by the Department of Transport.
Finance, loans, etc., by a bank manager of Vancouver.
International agreements, by a commissioner of the international salmon commission.

Income tax and record keeping, by a man from the income tax department.
Marine insurance, by the treasurer of an insurance company.
Economics, by one of our economists in the department.
Markets and distribution, by the sales manager of one of our largest fishing companies.
Boat design and construction, by a naval architect.
Panel on fisheries education in Japan, because the Japanese are our great competitors in the north Pacific.
The course was so successful that the fishermen's unions and industry have all asked for a larger course next year and requests have now come from other areas for a similar course to be given to their fishermen. Cost of the course was $3,000, the department providing free tuition, transportation and board.
The last thing I should like to touch on is something which is not generally spoken of in fisheries debates in the House of Commons, the sports fishing of Canada. The B.N.A. Act gives the federal government complete control over fishing in Canada but over the years we have worked out a very satisfactory arrangement for eight of the 10 provinces whereby they administer the sports fishing in conjunction with their game departments. It has worked out well. It is hard to estimate the value to Canada of sports fishing. We have had a tremendous increase in the number of sports fishermen. We see it best perhaps through the sale of sports fishing gear, which is greater than the combined sale of all gear for golf, tennis, and winter sports. We, however, control sports fishing in tidal waters, and in rivers of the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, and British Columbia, on what are called the anadromous fish, fish that come in from the sea to spawn, of which salmon is the principal one.
On the west coast we have great sports fishing for salmon in the sea. We have big salmon derbies and competitions by people in rowboats. The biggest one had 15,000 people go out for a one-day fishing for prizes. Last year we had 144 of these salmon derbies sponsored by clubs, unions, boards of trade and towns. The total catch of salmon by sports fishermen approaches a quarter of a million fish, as far as we can estimate. It is an excellent thing as far as creating interest in the whole fishing industry. We have reserved certain areas for sports fishermen. Relations between the commercial fishermen and the sports fishermen are excellent. On the west
[Mr. Sinclair.!
coast we have two or three special areas reserved entirely for sports fishing. These are three areas where the tyee salmon, a very large form of spring salmon, is the principal fish. They are Campbell river, Phillips Arm and River inlet. The River inlet breeds the largest race of salmon in Canada. I was there last summer one day, and in that day 94 salmon, averaging 43 pounds, were caught. The largest was 86 pounds.
On the east coast the salmon is not nearly as numerous but it is even more highly regarded as a sporting fish. In the last two years we have formed a committee of our department and the provincial departments to conserve and extend the Atlantic salmon fisheries. There are great problems in connection with it such as the increase in industrialization of the east coast, power dams, industrial pollution and spraying for spruce budworm. I hope the spraying is killing the spruce budworm as effectively as it kills all insect life in the streams in which the baby salmon live.
I realize that I have not covered all the activities of the department, but those matters not covered can be raised on the individual items.
I do not want to interrupt the minister but may I ask him whether there is any indication that what is being used to combat the spruce budworm has affected the fish at all?

Yes. For instance, in the South Miramichi the company that sprayed there-I will not mention the name of the company-used half a gallon of DDT per acre. Our scientists examined the streams and found that the spray had killed completely all insect life in the streams. There are no nymphs, larvae, worms or small flies, as a consequence of which the small Atlantic salmon which live in these streams the first three years all die of starvation. Mind you, if these areas were not sprayed for spruce budworm the trees would have died and there would have been no cover for insects anyway. It is one of those things that have to be done. Our job is to restore the fisheries once the spraying is over.
To summarize the statistics of our department, may I say that this year's estimate is for $12,044,963, down $344,211 from last year despite salary increases and the application of the 40-hour week to our 75 patrol vessels. Our revenue is $256,473 out of licences and confiscation of fish plus the $1 million from seal skins. Our staff is composed of 1,562 permanent, 736 seasonal and 17 part-time employees, making a total of 2,315. That is up 55 from last year, mostly seasonal, in our inspection and in our protection services.

I should like to close by paying tribute to the staff of the department. This year we lost Stewart Bates who had been deputy minister for 10 years. He did a magnificent job in organizing the Department of Fisheries. When he left he was chairman of the North Pacific commission, chairman of the North Atlantic commission and he would have been chairman of the great international fisheries conference which met in Rome this spring. He was a good man and he trained a good staff. The promotions to deputy minister and assistant deputy came from within the department. I am proud of the type of person we have in the Department of Fisheries. They do not get as big pay as those mentioned in the bills we were discussing but these scientists of ours and officials are men who-to use the phrase used by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-find that their vocation is their avocation. They are happy in their work. It is great work, scientific research, engineering, protection, marketing. They are close to nature. They are conserving a great national resource. I can tell you as Minister of Fisheries that I am glad to head the department and that, in my opinion, for a person of my inclinations, my job is the best one in the cabinet.

Mr. Chairman, whatever else one might say of the minister or in the way of criticism of his administration of his department, I am sure that no one could ever criticize the manner in which he delivers his opening report on the first item. He has a colourful and dramatic manner of delivery and he seems almost to make the report live. I am sure he must have been born within sight of the sea and that he must have read Joseph Conrad a great deal as a boy because you can almost smell the salt air and sometimes even get the smell of curing fish as he describes the work of his department.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to review at any length the statement made by the minister because I think, as he said, most of these matters can be dealt with more effectively when we come to the various headings of his department. But I should like to discuss the department generally for a few minutes, and with particular reference to one or two matters which,

frankly, are of special interest to the fishermen of eastern Canada. I am perfectly prepared to admit I have no special knowledge-in fact, I have no knowledge whatsoever except that which one gets from reading the newspapers-of fisheries in western Canada and on the Pacific coast, and I would not attempt to deal with them in any way at all.
The minister did make an interesting statement and announcement of policy this morning with respect to the subsidy or drawback which is going to be given to what one might call the salt fishermen, those who are using salt in the processing of their fish. I am glad he did that at that time because I had intended to speak for a little while about the policy that has been followed by the department up to now. We had some special subsidies paid to the salt fish trade of Newfoundland and, as the minister knows, that caused some criticism in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. As I said, I had intended to speak about that but now it is not necessary because we have the announcement of a different policy entirely. I do not intend to discuss that policy now because I have not had an opportunity to consider it. However, I understand from the minister there will be a supplementary vote with respect thereto, and we can deal with it at that time.
I am very glad to see that this has been done. With all due respect to the fish trade of Newfoundland, no matter what arguments may be used in support, the fact is that it is not helpful to have special benefits applying to one province as against other provinces competing in the same trade. I know the fishermen of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were somewhat critical of that last year. If there is any danger now of Newfoundland seceding from Canada it is probably just as well that we do not pay them any money because if we have to lose them we do not want them to take our money with them. The minister has adopted a fairly happy expedient to get away from that.
As he has told us, there was a larger catch of fish last year, and on the whole I think the fishing industry is in a relatively satisfactory condition. Bearing in mind what he said, in my opinion the fishing industry in the east is one where the men risk more, work harder and get less than in any other trade or industry in which they could engage. If there is some slight increase in their standard of living or degree of prosperity, then it is certainly one they have earned and one which they well deserve.
