I think there are two main problems in the fishing industry. Some of us listened in another place yesterday to the discussion of the plans for rehabilitation of the fishing industry. I may refer to that later, but generally speaking there is the problem of conservation and the problem of marketing. The minister referred to the various international treaties and international commissions through which so much has been done during the last few years towards the conservation of the fishing industry. I think much more has to be done. I think the minister deserves credit for what has been done this year in connection with the great lakes international convention. I think it will go a long way towards the conservation of the fishing industry of the great lakes. It is simply an experiment at the moment. We are starting out on something which is badly needed and which we trust will result in satisfactory dividends in the long run.
We have, of course, the northwest Atlantic *convention dealing with the fisheries in the northwestern Atlantic. But when we read the reports of the fisheries research board, Dr. Needler's statements and others, I think we are all impressed with the fact that there is a threat even to the fish population of that tremendous body of water which, as the minister said this morning, has been fished for over 500 years. When you get foreign trawlers coming there, dragging in pairs, catching young haddock and engaging in various other fishing enterprises which are certainly inimical to the life of the industry, I think something should be done and the minister should see to it that the various nations engaged in that industry should, through conventions or otherwise, do more towards the safeguarding of it than is being done at the moment.
On the marketing end I know that we have engaged in advertising to a substantial extent. We also have a household economics branch in an adjacent building where most valuable work has been done in trying to induce the people of Canada to use more fish by showing them how well fish can be prepared. I am sure if all the people of Canada had the opportunity to go to the household economics kitchens in the west block and taste fish as it is cooked there, part of the problem of the fishing industry would be solved very quickly. One sees there what can be done, and unfortunately it is not being done throughout Canada as a whole. Why, I cannot understand.
I know that the Canadian National Railways is making an effort in this direction and that "Canex" fish, specially treated fish, is
(Mr. Nowlan.]
being carried on their trains at the moment; but there is something about it that apparently does not appeal to the Canadian public. It is an unfortunate circumstance that we, a nation bordering on the Atlantic and the Pacific and having the greatest fishing industry in the world, still eat much less fish than almost any other people in the world. Surely there must be some way in which this challenge can be met. I believe the minister told us last year that if only a few more pounds of fish per head of population could be consumed by the Canadian people the future of the fishing industry would be solved, but with the advertising, with everything else that is being done, we still have not solved the problem. I know it is a challenge to the minister and I suggest to him that something more must be done. I am not trying to make concrete suggestions. Frankly, I do not know what they are any more than the minister probably does, but I do know there is a challenge there and an opportunity, and we should pursue the matter further than we are doing today.
On the other side there is, of course, our export market. The minister mentioned this morning that our sales to the United States had fallen off slightly. He condoned that and said that it is a very good thing because we do not want to have all our fish in the one basket. That is perfectly true, but nevertheless the United States market has been a tremendous market for us, and it should be. Last night I happened to glance at the minister's optimistic speech of a year ago, and it was an optimistic speech. The minister always makes optimistic speeches. In his speech last year he emphasized particularly the development of the fish stick phase of the industry. He told us what wonderful possibilities there were in that and how he hoped it would go a long way towards solving the problems of the Canadian fishermen.
What is the situation in that respect? I notice that he did not tell us anything about that today. My understanding is that as a result of the imposition of a tariff by the United States that promising market which the minister foresaw last year has been largely closed to us.
Would the hon. member permit a correction? I did give the very great increase in the production of fishsticks totalling altogether 33 million pounds last year.
Of fillets?
Of fillets in frozen blocks.

That is quite true. As I was going to say, we are undoubtedly sending

fillets into the United States for manufacture into fishsticks, as the minister has said. It is a tremendous outlet for us but what we were talking about last year, and what the minister was talking about was the possibility of exporting the fishsticks themselves to the United States. We are faced with a situation now where there is a tariff of 30 per cent, I think it is, on the cooked fishsticks and 20 per cent on the uncooked fishsticks. The rather terrifying thing is that a year ago the United States tariff commission received representations from the New England fishing industry that a tariff should be imposed against us. The President of the United States refused to implement that recommendation. We are told now that congress has passed legislation which will impose a duty of 30 per cent on the cooked fishsticks and 20 per cent on the uncooked and that, subject to certain negotiations, so far as Canada is concerned that tariff will be effective against us. Of course, it is effective today because the Canadian fishing industry, knowing that a tariff is overhanging the situation like a cloud, has wisely decided they cannot meet it.
As the minister says, we are now engaged in sending the fillets into the United States rather than the fishsticks themselves. We are thankful for the market for fillets. However, I get somewhat tired, Mr. Chairman, of hearing someone say all the time that we must not do anything to antagonize the United States; that we could lose the market for Canadian fish. Certainly we do not want to lose that market, but I doubt very much if there is any great danger of that happening. After all, the United States is becoming more and more dependent every year upon Canada for raw materials and some manufactured products. The commission which recently reported to the United States government emphasized that fact. Therefore, I do not believe, provided we act reasonably, we have to worry too much about retaliation. We should stand on our own rights. We got a reduction in the tariff on pickled herring, which is of some importance, from one-half cent a pound to one-quarter cent a pound. Then, we had the imposition of the duty on fishsticks as against that.
In so far as fillets are concerned, what are they paying? I believe the duty is one and a quarter cents per pound for a certain quota and two and a half cents per pound above that quota. We are not getting any free access to the United States market at all. Frankly, we are paying through the nose. We are paying a cent and a quarter a pound on the price the fisherman gets for that fish, which is a relatively high tariff. As I said,
Supply-Fisheries
I think that is one of the problems with which the department has to deal. We have to try to develop the export market even more than it is today. Certainly, if the United States fishing industry had its way they would erect a tariff against us as high as Haman's gallows, as they proved last year when the New England fishing industry made these representations to the United States tariff commission. The situation is different today from what it was a few years ago. I think our government can take a stand with respect to that, and I think the minister has the courage to do that. It is something that I think needs to be done in the future.
Something was said this morning about the rehabilitation of the industry. Of course, there are two phases of this rehabilitation, as I see it. I look at this through bifocal glasses because I am living in a territory where we have inshore fishermen, the ones who are going out in the morning and coming back at night. They are my constituents. They are the ones I know personally, and the ones I know best. Their problem is not so much that of rehabilitation, as the minister explained yesterday to the committee on banking and commerce when we were dealing with another matter. In so far as the offshore fishermen are concerned, it is true that they need larger boats and better boats and some of the equipment of which he told us this morning. I think this bill to provide loans to fishermen is a step in the right direction. It has been needed in the past by these fishermen. Yesterday representatives of the fishermen and the fishermen's credit unions from all over Canada appeared before the committee. Certainly, those who had not met them before were impressed by the character and ability of these men who have done so much towards the financial uplift of the fishing industry. I think of organizations like the united maritime fishermen, the credit unions of Nova Scotia and the co-operative unions; they all fought for the fishermen 20 years ago, and the position in which the fishermen and the fishing industry find themselves today is the result of their work. As these loans are made available, larger boats and better equipment will be bought. Then, these fishermen can undoubtedly do a better job in this modern and highly industrialized industry than was the case before.
The inshore fishermen still use the methods which were used many years ago. They have to do that because fishing there is somewhat restricted. They live in little villages, go out in the morning and come back at night. They have not the high seas to contend with. Their problems are entirely different. They are

Supply-Fisheries
faced with the challenge of this industrialization; they are faced with the problem of the trawler and the dragger. Some day I hope to have the minister along the shore visiting these fishing villages and listening to the bitterness with which the fishermen refer to these trawlers that come in and, as they put it, ruin their fishing grounds and destroy their livelihood. There may be some overemphasis; there may be some bias in their point of view. The offshore fishermen say that old methods must give way to new, but these people in these villages, who have lived there generation after generation, should be given more protection than they were in the past.
A short time ago I noticed that the minister or his department issued regulations restricting the use of trawlers in St. Margaret's bay off Halifax. There were protests galore from fishermen and from one or two organizations. I believe the minister went down there just before the provincial election. I might say he almost ran into a barrage of rifle fire from these people who were-
It was a coincidence.

It was no coincidence, without any question, that I was there two days before the minister came; it was an amazing political coincidence. At any rate, we all sent protests and the department substantially restricted the operation of trawlers in that bay.
I say to him now that the same thing should be done in St. Mary's bay, which is no larger. The Acadian fishermen living along the borders of that bay say their livelihood is being completely destroyed by these trawlers.
I have here-I am not reading any newspaper article, Mr. Chairman-certain newspaper stories. I have one, for instance, from Tiverton, which is in my constituency, to the effect that a short time ago three fishermen lost their gear in one day, not only because of United States trawlers operating within the 12 mile limit but also because of Canadian trawlers operating within that limit. They lost their trawls and all their gear. According to this newspaper story they say they are going to take rifles out into the bay of Fundy in order to defend themselves against the depradations of these trawlers. One would think that we were away back to the days of Captain Kidd and the pirates of old, of the old Spanish main. We have the strangest situation in the world down there. As we know, Canadian trawlers over 65 feet long are supposed to stay out more than 12 miles from the Canadian coast line. They have to meet our regulations. On the other hand, American trawlers are allowed to come within three miles of our coast line. How can you explain an inconsistent situation like that? It cannot be done.

So far as our inshore fishermen are concerned, they want them both out 12 miles, for their own protection. The Canadians are kept beyond the 12 mile limit and the Americans are allowed within three miles- and on a dark foggy night they may come in within 300 yards of the shore, and sweep up the lobster traps along that shore, as has happened time and again. No wonder the fishermen are irritated.
This morning the minister referred to the international law commission of the United Nations. I was glad he did, because in my opinion that is the most important thing which has developed this year, so far as the fishing industry is concerned. If a good catch of fish this year is to depend upon Providence and the Minister of Fisheries, then the minister is responsible to some extent for the fishing industry; it is between him and Providence. The Social Credit government took responsibility for the oil industry in Alberta, so the minister and Providence may take the responsibility for the condition of the fishing industry. But the one thing that is important is the report of the international law commission. As I understand it some United Nations organization some time ago-I am not sure when-appointed an international law commission to consider the problem of the shore line. It was to decide what were coastal waters and what were not coastal waters.
As the minister said, we know that certain countries extended them, and they got into trouble with the United States. Perhaps the result was that they lost markets. Our government, wisely I think, has waited for the report of the commission. I see in the newspapers of the last few days that that commission has reported, but I have not yet seen a copy of the report. I presume the minister has it, and I would hope that he would make it available.
According to that report the international law commission recommends that the coastal waters should extend 12 miles from all coast lines. I trust that means from headland to headland, rather than following the indentations of shore lines. As the minister has said, some years ago we had an interdepartmental committee working on that matter, and I believe Dean Curtis was chairman. I presume that committee has reported to the government and the minister. I suggest the minister should tell us what the report of the committee is, and should place before us the recommendations of Dean Curtis. We would like to know the stand the government will take with respect to it, because on that depends, I think, the future of at least our

inshore fishermen. And since we now have the authority of an international association such as the United Nations, and since a committee of that organization has recommended-apparently unanimously-that coast lines be extended to 12 miles, then I am suggesting to the minister that our government should take action. We should not wait to have it adopted by the United Nations; because, after all, the United Nations is composed of large and powerful groups. It is a somewhat ponderous organization, and perhaps the mechanism which it would bring into play would be even more ponderous than some think is that of the House of Commons.
With the authority of that international organization, and with the study of our own interdepartmental committee-if that study is along the same line-I think our minister should instruct our Secretary of State for External Affairs to approach the American government with a view to instituting negotiations now, so that we may have the situation clarified in the relatively near future.
Because this situation cannot go on. It is an impossible situation when you have Canadian fishermen kept out beyond the 12 mile limit and the American fishermen coming within three miles-and the inshore fishermen being ruined by both. So far as I am concerned, representing the inshore fishermen, while I would not wish to see the Canadian trawlers suffer any injustice, I would with all my strength fight any proposal that either should come within the three mile limit. Both of them should be kept out beyond 12 miles, and then we can give some protection to the inshore fishermen.
The hon. member for Charlotte and I look at the subject from the standpoint of the bay of Fundy fishermen. If we had an agreement stipulating a distance of 12 miles, headland to headland, the situation in the bay of Fundy would be much different from what it is today. This is something which should receive the attention of the Secretary of State for External Affairs-because I am sure the Minister of Fisheries is familiar with it, and the record is there. According to our contention the bay of Fundy is a coastal water, anyway. Discussions were carried on around 1840 or 1850, before we became a nation, at which time the secretary of state of the United States said that the bay of Fundy was part of the high seas. The colonial secretary for Great Britain said that they were coastal waters. Many long letters passed back and forth, and they finally agreed to leave the matter as an open question.
Supply-Fisheries
Neither would admit the other was right. And the situation still stands at that point today.
Therefore, as I said, this is a most important matter-the most important step taken in the last while which could be of assistance to the fishing industry. I hope the minister will see to it that we do not have to wait for a very long time, until the conclusion of interminable discussions before the United Nations. The Americans are fair and sensible. Their officials are reasonable. The minister told us that last year-he said that he found that when they sat around the conference table they were fair and reasonable. I have no doubt about that at all.
Since they are fair and reasonable men, and since this is a problem with which we are confronted, and since we have the authority of the commission behind us, I am sure the minister and his representatives will be able to work out some modus vivendi whereby all the trawlers will be kept out beyond the 12 mile limit until such time as the United Nations Organization makes some definite finding in the matter which will be appropriate beyond peradventure.
I said at the outset that I did not wish to speak long. There is only one other matter which the minister did not touch, but which I think should be mentioned. Again, this is a matter of peculiar importance to my own constituency, where the fishermen go out in the morning and back at night. They have sailed those waters for three generations, and they do not go out of sight of land. Ships are sometimes lost in big storms, by act of God, but this does not happen often.
It now seems that they are to be subject to the possibility of action on the part of the Department of Transport by way of imposing regulations in connection with the inspection of boats. I know those regulations have been modified to some extent, and I know that studies are still going on. I have been supplied with copies of the new regulations. I understand that the boats of the scallop fleet, to which the minister referred this morning, will come within the purview of those regulations. It seems to me that they should not be compelled to adopt standards which are presumably applied to the boats which sail out on the high seas, when they go out in the morning and back at night. I hope the minister will keep a sort of jaundiced eye on this situation. I must say in passing that I give full credit to the officials of the Department of Transport who have been most reasonable in listening to the representations made. However, the regulations are still there, and the reply we

Supply-Fisheries
received was, "We will consider it." But we have to face this thing sooner or later.
We do not want to face it; because for a man to have to put in a copper water tank to go out on the bay of Fundy and back again is ridiculous. He has probably used a boat on those waters all his life, and his grandfather before him. For instance, to have to double the diameter of the drive shaft does not seem to him necessary at all. I was told by one of them, "If the drive shaft should break, we can always hoist a blanket and get ashore in 12 hours, as we have done many times." This is just an instance of, I was going to say bureaucracy, but that would be unkind; they have not been bureaucratic in their approach. On the contrary, they have been reasonable. But the matter has been hanging over their heads, and I want the minister to look into it.
Has not a man the right to risk his own life?
We presume that is one of our privileges. I shall not take the time of the committee any longer. There are other matters which we will take up when the individual items are before us.

Mr. Chairman, in the relatively short time during which I have been a member of this house I have tried wherever possible to make myself familiar with the operations of the Department of Fisheries. Quite frankly, as one who sits on the opposite side of the house from the government, I think it is quite proper wherever justified to offer constructive criticism of the operations of the department. However, I believe it is also the responsibility of a member on the opposite side to give credit when he believes that credit is due.
My opinion is that most of the steps which have been taken by the Department of Fisheries since I became a member of the house have been in the right direction although there may have been times when they did not go as far as I would have liked. At the outset of my remarks, which will not be too extended, I should like to say that the opinion expressed earlier by the minister in regard to the type of people he has as officials in his department is shared by me as a result of such contacts as I have had with them. The minister mentioned particularly some of those in senior positions in the department, but if I were going to supplement his remarks in that respect I would say that I have found the officials in the field with whom I have come in contact to be genuinely interested in doing a good job. They have been ready to inform one as a member of parliament of the problems they were

facing. I think it can be said that generally speaking the morale throughout the whole Department of Fisheries is good today, and I agree with the minister's suggestion that the recently retired deputy minister had much to do with this.
I join in the remarks of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings in his reference to the test kitchen operated by the department. Hon. members may recall that on one occasion when I had returned from sampling what could be produced there I drew to the attention of hon. members particulars of what could be done. I agree with the hon. member when he says that there is still a great deal to be done to instruct the people of Canada in the further use of our various fish products.
I had occasion fairly recently, in a place which shall remain nameless, to sample lake Superior lake trout, a fish which had been suggested during the hearings on an international convention to be the prize fish of the great lakes. I must say that after that sample I was moved to make the facetious remark that perhaps we should .let this fish go back to the lamprey eel. I must say again that I do agree with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that there is a good deal to be done in showing the Canadian people how they can best use the resources of our seas.
I think because of the very richness of those resources, as was suggested this morning by the minister, we have as a nation failed to appreciate the tremendous resource that we have. Perhaps that is partly true because of the richness of the land heritage which we as a small nation of people have in our hands, and perhaps it is partly due to the fact that except for that portion of our population which has been living immediately adjacent to our seashores there has been little appreciation of that value during the years of Canadian history. We have at this stage of our history a better opportunity to utilize that resource to greater advantage over a longer period of our history than might otherwise be the case.
I think most hon. members will agree that Canada is not likely to remain a country of empty spaces forever. As we move on into the future more and more of our land resources which are easily available will tend to be fully utilized or partially exhausted and we will perhaps come to rely in a much more basic degree than we do at the present time upon the resources of the sea.
I imagine that other hon. members have seen a recent issue of Maclean's magazine which featured the celebration of their fiftieth anniversaries by the provinces of Alberta

and Saskatchewan. Hon. members may have been interested, as I was, in that part of the issue which described the building up of the prairies from a geological point of view. One point which struck me more than any other was that the great wealth of our prairie provinces had come almost in its entirety from the sea, of course over a period of many millions of years. I have been thinking that while we inherited that accumulated store of richness out of the submergence of that area under the sea at various periods of geological time, as we exhaust that perhaps we will have to become increasingly aware that all around us lies that same sort of richness in the living sea where it will be renewed from year to year, provided we are prepared to make proper use of it.
1 have been glad to note that during this session of parliament more of the legislative program has been devoted or related to the people who toil to bring in our fish. Perhaps that is an indication that there is a more general recognition across the country of the real importance of our fisheries to Canada as a whole. As a member of the industrial relations committee I was interested in the sessions that were held in connection with unemployment insurance for fishermen, and I think out of that discussion there arose within the membership of that committee a better understanding of some of the problems faced by the people who make their living in this industry. Behind the statistics of the number of pounds of fish caught, the market value of the production, the percentage of the production going into export and the need for greater home consumption must be a realization that the fishing industry is really the people who do the fishing.
The interest that was shown in the industrial relations committee in respect to those people, I felt to be a very encouraging sign. That also, I feel, applies to the bill presently under discussion in relation to making it easier for fishermen to obtain the necessary credit to improve their operations. The discussion in the banking and commerce committee, which was referred to by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, in respect to making use of the fishermen's own credit unions was a very encouraging sign, particularly because of the general appreciation that seemed to come from members from all quarters of the house in that connection.
Like other members, I was very much interested in the rather complete outline that the minister gave us of some of the activities of the department, relating as they did, among other things, to the program of research and the attempts at conservation being conducted by the fisheries research board. I noted that
Supply-Fisheries
he made mention of the mid-water trawl development on the Pacific coast. During the luncheon recess I happened to notice an item in that connection in one of my local newspapers. Perhaps an indication that the department in this field of research development is reaching out into the unknown was the fact that this idea of a mid-water trawl is still so new that the headline of the newspaper read, "Mid-winter trawl", where it should have said, "Mid-water trawl".
I have been quite interested, too, in the continuing program for the improvement of the facilities of our migrating salmon to reach their spawning grounds. Naturally, as the member for Comox-Alberni, I was greatly interested in the recent opening of the new and improved fishways in the Stamp falls section of the Somass river system. That particular river, I understand, is the most important salmon spawning stream which enters the ocean on the western coast of Vancouver island, and undoubtedly that improvement will be welcomed in years to come by the fishermen who make their living from the fish that spawn in that river.
I was interested in the remarks the minister made this morning in connection with the co-operative effort to use our rivers both for purposes of power and as salmon spawning streams. That, of course, has been a subject of considerable interest in another committee of this house during the current session and is certainly one that is going to be of great continuing interest to all members from the province of British Columbia. I can agree with the minister that, generally speaking, there is recognition of the importance of that co-operative consideration being given in respect to the establishment of such major projects as power dams. On the other hand, it has appeared to me from pieces of information I have picked up here and there that whilst that may be the case, that in respect to salmon spawning streams along the British Columbia coast, many of which are comparatively small and yet still make a substantial contribution to the over-all plenitude of salmon in our Pacific waters, some of our spawning ground opportunities are going by the board. Perhaps this is partly due to the general ignorance of the manner in which those streams are used by the salmon. I have heard of cases where people, quite unaware of the fact that they were doing any damage, would remove gravel from stream beds which had been carrying salmon eggs. I know, of course, that the officers of this department, wherever that sort of thing comes to their attention, take the necessary steps to correct the situation. On the other hand I sometimes

Supply-Fisheries
wonder whether or not the divided jurisdiction which exists is causing us to lose some of our salmon spawning ground as a result of the logging activities that take place in British Columbia.
The minister mentioned that fishing is under federal jurisdiction, and we all know that our forest resources are under provincial jurisdiction. From bits of conversation here, and observations there, I am forming an impression that in many ways, whilst the power of the Fisheries Act, as I understand it, is there to prevent spoiling of salmon spawning grounds through logging activities, in many cases a good deal of damage is done before any officer of the department is aware that it has been done. The minister has referred to the field of education, and I have wondered whether there is not room for exploration of the possibilities of more education among the people of the logging fraternity of British Columbia on this question. As I understand it, in the prairie provinces officials of the provincial governments receive appointments as federal fisheries officers. I am wondering whether some arrangement could be made whereby our British Columbia forest service officers, for whom I personally have quite a high regard, could in effect be made fisheries officers also. Perhaps more than I am aware has been done in that direction. Nevertheless, if some arrangement of that kind could be worked out, there might be a greater sense of responsibility for directing logging operations in such a way that the drying up of the smaller spawning streams and the creating of obstructions in them would not be as common as it has been reported to me is the case.
Speaking of the field of education, I should like at this point to say that, as one of the members who saw the other day the production of the fisheries department through the national film board, that is a type of educational undertaking of which I certainly approve most heartily. To all members who have . a taste for lobster I would recommend that they avail themselves of any opportunity to get a bird's eye glimpse of the private life of the lobster which that film affords. I might also say that I have heard some favourable reports of the program of education to which the minister referred and which has been carried out in British Columbia. The syllabus he gave was much more complete than I had realized it to be. From various things I have read and heard I know that some of the courses have been well received by many of the fishermen.
In his remarks with regard to sports fishing, the minister referred to the fact that in much of the British Columbia coastal area we have
important sports fisheries on the salt water and he also made the remark that the relationships between the sports fishermen and the commercial fishery interests were excellent.
Except in one part of your riding.

That may be quite true, generally speaking, but nevertheless I think the minister will agree that on occasion there are some exceptions and that problems arise which create certain conflicts of interest in that direction. He mentioned the fact that certain areas have been set aside exclusively for sports fishermen. He is probably well aware of the fact that from time to time, as our tourist industry in places like Vancouver island increases, the demands for increased sports areas create certain problems that are not always too easy to resolve. I raise the point because I feel that it is important that such difficulties be equitably resolved before the occurrence of any real break in that relationship which he described.
I was interested in the minister's brief reference to the operations of the fisheries prices support board. I understand that he may have something further to say on that matter when we come to that particular item. I think I might perhaps make one or two references to the subject now in order that the minister may be informed of what is and has been in my mind in this connection. In order to do that, I should like to preface my remarks by reference to some figures which I have gleaned from the 1951 census. I realize that the picture presented there has been modified somewhat since then. But I also understand that the 1951 census gave a much more complete picture of the fishing industry than had ever been given before. I therefore assume that it is considered to be a good basic reference for fishery statistics, at least until the next volumes of the census appear.
I have done a bit of gleaning from the pages of the volume on fisheries and I feel that the figures presented there reveal some rather interesting contrasts within the fishing industry and also in its relationship to the general economy at that time. I think that some of the steps that I agreed have been in the right direction that have been taken since 1951 have probably modified the situation somewhat for the better.
I was interested in noting that in that year the landed weight of grey cod-which I take to be the cod which is caught on the Atlantic shores-was 746,089,000 pounds and that in the same year the landed weight of Pacific salmon-the total of all species, I take it-was 169,098,000 pounds. That would

indicate that the Atlantic cod fishery was a much larger and perhaps much more important fishery than our Pacific salmon fishery. However, if one relates those figures to the landed value of the product, one gets a rather surprising result.
To me it was slightly startling to discover that the landed weight of Atlantic fish- which is between three and four times as large as that of our Pacific salmon-was valued at only $18,574,000 whereas our 169,098,000 pounds of Pacific salmon were worth $24,887,000.
If my calculations are correct, they reveal that the approximate value per pound of the cod was 2i cents whereas that of the Pacific salmon was about 14J cents. These figures explained to me many of the things which I observed when I was for a time on the Atlantic coast in the province of Newfoundland last fall, and they revealed to me why some of the problems that I heard of as being the problems of Newfoundland were what they are.
I was also interested to note that, according to the same census figures, the number of fishermen in Newfoundland was 19,556 and that the landed value of all the fishery products was $15,177,000 whereas in British Columbia there are shown to be 6,715 fishermen, with a landed value of all fishery products of $33,991,000. Nova Scotia is in between with 10,504 fishermen, and with a landed value of all fishery products of $21,308,000. Again, if my feeble arithmetic is correct, that means that in Newfoundland the average return per fisherman was $770 in that year, in Nova Scotia, $2,028, and in British Columbia, $5,061. These figures reveal to me an interesting contrast. I point out immediately, of course, that these figures, as I understand it, do not represent only the actual wage return to that number of fishermen. To me at least they reveal that in British Columbia a much larger proportion of the landed value of the catch goes into the mechanized equipment and the other costs of operation to which the minister was referring this morning.
There are 53,995 persons listed as engaged in the fishing industry across the country. The landed value of their catch totalled $109,136,000 and there was other income in the industry amounting to $18,831,000, making a total of $127,967,000. Taking these figures, the gross income per fisherman works out at $2,370. Deducting from gross income the amount of $43,552,000 for expenditures, we have a net return of $84,415,000, or an average return per fisherman of $1,567 across Canada. Again, I would point out that this figure does not represent only the amount 50433-328
Supply-Fisheries
received in wages by the fisherman but is comprised of wages and the profits taken by the various fishing enterprises, large and small.
Therefore it appears to me that these figures substantiate the statement that the fisherman has not been getting his fair share compared with the average return received by Canadian workers. I think these things should be borne in mind when one considers the operations of the fisheries prices support board. It may be recalled that in connection with the study of unemployment insurance the suggestion was made in the brief of the commission that perhaps some further consideration should be given to making greater use of the fisheries prices support board principle. I think perhaps some of the deductions that can be made from the figures to which I have referred indicate that is the case.
I recall that earlier this year when we were debating the amendment and renewal of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act I drew attention to the fact that there were approximately the same number of workers employed in the gold mining industry in Canada as are engaged in fishing in the province of Newfoundland. I referred to the fact that a direct government subsidy of around $14 million was being paid to the gold mining industry, and that one of the arguments advanced at that time was that such payment would assist in maintaining employment in that industry. Perhaps that is not altogether relevant, except to support my contention that the fishermen have not been getting more than their fair share by way of return for their work.
The figures I have quoted suggest that, relatively speaking, the fishermen of British Columbia are perhaps better off than their cousins on the Atlantic shores. Yet I know from my own experience that apart from the particularly successful individual, the fishermen of British Columbia have in many cases not been making more than a decent living, and in many other cases a good deal less from their work in the industry. When the minister suggested this morning that the Fisheries Prices Support Act was never intended to supplement general low prices on the world market I was interested in his statement, because it seemed to me to be somewhat at variance with statements found at the beginning of the annual report of the fisheries prices support board for 1953-54. The opening paragraph of that report reads in part as follows:
The act which came into force in July, 1947, gives the fisheries prices support board the usual powers of a government corporation; provides a working fund of $25 million . . .

Supply-Fisheries
In dealing with the $14 million paid to the gold mining industry in the debate on the amendment to that act, I pointed out that the further supplementary estimates for the year 1954-55 contained an item of $744,382 to recoup the fisheries prices support account to cover the net operating loss for the completed program of the fisheries prices support board as of March 31, 1955. Therefore both in relation to the $14 million in connection with the gold mining industry and the working fund of $25 million of the fisheries prices support board, the actual scale of operation of the fisheries prices support board would appear to have been comparatively small. The report of the fisheries prices support board sets out that there are two methods that may be used to support prices of fisheries products, and goes on to say:
These methods are (a) the purchase of any fisheries product at a prescribed price and (b) the making of deficiency payments to producers of a fisheries product equal to the difference between a prescribed price and the average price at which such product was sold during a specified period. The act furthermore directs that in prescribing prices the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for fisheries by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries and those from other occupations.
The last phrase in particular, "and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from fisheries and those from other occupations", suggests to me that there is a difference between the policy stated there and the statement made by the minister this morning that the Fisheries Prices Support Act was never intended to supplement general low prices.
From the little personal observation I have had the opportunity of making, and from the picture revealed to me by these statistics- particularly the contrast between the price for Pacific salmon, 14J cents a pound, and the price for cod, 2J cents a pound-and even with the contrast between the price fishermen on the west coast get for such fresh cod as they do bother to bring in and the existing situation under which fish fillets from Newfoundland and the other maritime areas are sold, I believe more might have been done through the medium of the fisheries prices support board than apparently has been done. Now, that is not to say that I do not agree-

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman; I had not been watching the clock as closely as I should. I was on the point of concluding.

I was going to say that I agree with the outline the minister gave of the steps that are being taken to develop better markets, better products and all that sort of thing; but without an improvement in the existing price level, and expecting fishermen to have resources out of which they can improve their own equipment, I feel that perhaps greater consideration could be given to the use of the fisheries prices support board set-up.

I should like first of all, Mr. Chairman, to thank the minister for the very able and interesting manner in which he presented the review of the activities of his department, and also commend him for the energy and diligence with which he fulfils the responsibilities that are his. I say that, of course, with this reservation, that even though we recognize the diligence and the energy he applies and the interest he takes in the work of his department, there are some things with which we do not altogether agree.
I should like to say how much we appreciate the films that have been shown during this session of parliament. They certainly have enabled some of us who live in one part of the country to gain some understanding of the nature of fishing operations as well as the problems facing fishermen in other parts of the country. Personally I have appreciated that opportunity of gaining information along those lines. It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to go into the details with respect to the administration of the department or criticisms of the department. I should like to make a few general observations on the fishing industry.
In the course of his remarks this morning the Minister of Fisheries reviewed some of the various treaties and conventions that had been put into operation to safeguard the fishing industry and to develop our fish resources. He mentioned as well the fact that we are reaching the point where we are pretty well ringed with these treaties.
I believe the success that has been achieved by these various agreements and treaties has certainly indicated that they have been worth while. In so far as the agreement concerning the sea lamprey menace on the great lakes is concerned, with which we dealt a short time ago, we recognize the tremendous need for such an agreement. We certainly urge the speedy implementation of any of those projects which will assist in the eradication of that menace.
Another item that has been of great interest, and I might say was a very welcome piece of legislation this session, was the measure concerning fishermen's loans. We are not

discussing that in this debate, of course, but I do feel it is something that is very much needed, considering the fact it is expected that some of the fishermen who operate in my area will be forced to go out into deeper water very soon. I trust this measure will enable them to make the necessary conversion of their gear and equipment in order to carry on their fishing operations.
It seems to me there is an increasing understanding of the importance of the fishing industry to the economy of our country. This has been shown in the different debates last session as well as this year, and it appears that a greater emphasis has been placed on these particular matters. Looking through the report of the Department of Fisheries and studying the various tables that have been included, the thought has come to my mind that there are many ways in which this industry is vital to the economy of Canada. I find that the number of fishermen stands at almost 80,000, and certainly that is a very important part of our population. I would feel, therefore, that anything that is done to promote and safeguard the industry will be in the best interests of the national economy from the viewpoint of employment.
Then, too, the figures the minister gave us this morning relative to the income from this source would make it appear that very real importance should be placed upon the fishing activities of our nation. From the viewpoint of fish as a source of food, when we consider the amount of fish that has been taken during these past several years, and the fact that it is increasing from year to year, one realizes it does constitute a very important part of the food supply not only of our own country but of other countries.
We are happy over the fact that some of the marketing problems have been overcome during the past year. The minister has stated that there are no worrying surpluses at the moment. This sounds better than the situation in previous years, when there was a substantial supply of canned salmon, for instance, that could not be disposed of on the market.
I was interested in the remarks that were made in connection with marketing fish from the eastern part of Canada, the cod prepared for market as fish sticks. It seems that these are developments that should greatly increase the demand for our fisheries products, and we certainly welcome any of these things that assist in this respect. I feel that there is a real necessity for the development of our home market as well as the export markets.
I did not have the opportunity to verify this figure, but in my reading the other day it was brought to my attention that 60 per cent

One of the problems that has been emphasized both this session and last has been that of conservation. The very first paragraphs in the report of the Department of Fisheries for the year 1953-54 are as follows:
One of the important responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries is to maintain and develop fish stocks in Canada. Unless the proper safeguards are taken, large-scale capture and other factors, such as water-use projects, pollution, etc., reduce fish populations and result in lower annual returns to the industry.
Certain species of fish, such as Pacific salmon, Atlantic lobster and Atlantic salmon, are more valuable than others. To ensure that annual yields will continue at maximum levels, the department spends large sums of money each year to prevent the fishermen from taking too many fish and to implement measures leading to the production of larger stocks.
We fully recognize the necessity of conservation programs. I was just wondering, while the minister was making his statement this morning, whether he had given any further consideration to the proposed closures on the Fraser river which were announced last year. He did not make any reference to them. I trust, however, that as he has time to investigate the situation and consider the alternate proposals advanced by fishermen's unions and other interested parties, he will find it possible to change the proposed plan and still allow fishing in that part of the river between the New Westminster and Mission bridges, as in years past.
The matter of hydroelectric development concerns us particularly. The minister referred this morning to the necessity of having both fish and power. In view of the proposals, studies and surveys conducted in British Columbia I do not think it is necessary to urge the minister to exercise great care and study the situation from every viewpoint, so that as a result of these discussions he will be able to take steps which will ensure the preservation of our fishing industry.
The other day in another debate I referred to an article in one of the newspapers in which the Minister of Fisheries was quoted as saying that he did not know whether or not to be alarmed by some of these proposals. As I say, I believe he is aware of the situation and the dangers, and that he will give serious attention to these matters.
I was interested as well in his references to the research that is being carried on. We had reference to this matter also in the study of the convention on the great lakes fisheries, where research was being carried on to try to find uses for the more than 100 species

of fish existing in the great lakes for which, up to the present time, a market has not been found.
I was also interested in the minister's reference to the possible use of dogfish. This, as well, will be of great interest to the fishermen; and when the matter is worked out and uses are found for these particular species of fish it will mean much to the fishermen from the standpoint of income.
The reference to the fisheries course being given at the University of British Columbia was something of which I had not heard before, no doubt because of my own failure to study these various matters. There is no doubt that the fishing industry is being revolutionized. Certainly those proposing to make it their. vocation would do well to avail themselves of the facilities offered by such a course, so they may prepare themselves adequately for efficient participation in the industry. I am just wondering if there could not be an additional course for chefs, because certainly, as we go across the country and stop in at various restaurants, cafes and eating places, we are led to the belief that if such a course were made available, and used, the consumption of fish would greatly increase.
Start with our own cafeteria.

I had not intended to make reference to any particular place. I think the condition is fairly general across the country.
Generally speaking, the activities of the department are appreciated. Once again, however, 1 come back to what may be considered my pet theme in this regard. I hope there will be a reappraisal of the fishing situation in the Fraser river, in the particular area between the Pattullo bridge and the New Westminster bridge. I believe that would be greatly appreciated by the fishermen in that area.

Mr. Chairman, we who were privileged this morning to listen to the presentation made by the Minister of Fisheries heard, I believe, one of the finest displays of knowledge of the fishing industry that has been heard in the House of Commons in many, many years. I would say it was a very fine presentation and should convince those in the house who had not heard the minister discuss the subject before that the right man has been chosen to represent this country behind the iron curtain. I have no doubt he will do a first-class job for this country.
I realize that any criticism I have to offer should come immediately after what I have just said. I should like to deal briefly with

that part of the minister's remarks in which he discussed the assistance to be given those who are in the salt fish industry of this country. I agree that it is one branch of the industry which, perhaps, would need more assistance than any other branch. It is the branch in which the income is low. It involves long hours of work, and hard work. Those who cure their own fish are obliged to wait long periods of time before any income reaches their homes.
In his remarks, however, the minister stated that in 1953 the fisheries prices support board paid $1.25 a quintal-

Yes, $1.12 a quintal on dried fish cured in Newfoundland. There is no member in the house who will criticize that action. I would point out, however, that at that time Newfoundland got almost 100 per cent of the amount set aside for fisheries support. As the minister stated at a later point in his remarks, the other maritime provinces did not ask for that support.
Regardless of whether they asked or not, the fact is that nearly 100 per cent of the money used that year by the fisheries prices support board went to Newfoundland. The table the minister presented today indicates that the salt fish fishermen of the maritime provinces will be helped to the extent of 50 per cent in the purchase of salt. This is a wonderful idea; but when I looked over the figures I found that $375,000 goes to Newfoundland. There was only $125,000 left for the other three maritime provinces and Quebec. The $375,000 works out at 75 per cent of the amount to be expended for this very worth-while purpose. That is the percentage that goes to Newfoundland. Nova Scotia gets $80,000; New Brunswick gets $22,000; Prince Edward Island gets $3,500, and Quebec $19,000.
Reference has been made today to a recent speech by the premier of Newfoundland to the effect that he would not wish what I might call the old Canadians to regard Newfoundlanders as second-rate citizens. I think if he will look over the assistance that has been provided by the Department of Fisheries for fishermen in the maritime provinces he will not find the people of Newfoundland considered second-rate citizens. Again I say that I support any assistance that is given them, but I believe a formula could have been worked out whereby the distribution would have been more proportionate.
I believe this assistance being provided will encourage more fishermen in the other maritime provinces to salt their own catch, which would be financially to their advantage. In

many cases fish that are sold in the fresh state return only 1 or 1| cents a pound, whereas if they are processed by the fisherman and held until the fall or winter they may bring 10, 12 or 14 cents a pound. I know the fishermen in my county wil be pleased with this assistance and will take full advantage of it. At the present time there is a good run of pollock in the area, while other branches of the industry are unproductive. This will encourage those who are engaged in that particular branch of the industry to process more fish in their own fish houses with the result that their income will be three times as great as it would be if they sold the fish in the fresh state.
There is one other criticism I have to offer with regard to the decrease in the amount being provided in the estimates this year for consumer services. I believe every fisherman who has knowledge of what this particular branch has been doing will regret this decrease. The demonstrations put on by the Department of Fisheries kitchen in the west block have been worth-while. I have attended two or three of the luncheons provided by that kitchen, and I know that every hon. member who has had the same experience has come away feeling they were doing a fine job for this country.
The booklets, cook books and pamphlets being put out by this department are appreciated by every housewife who has received one. I distributed quite a number to friends of mine, and in every case the answer was that there was more information in connection with the cooking and processing of fish than had been contained in any pamphlet previously issued. Originally the amount of this vote was $75,000, but it is being decreased by $13,500. Instead of being decreased this vote should have been increased by $25,000 this year, by $25,000 the following year and so on in order that the good work this branch of the department has been doing could be kept up.
One other suggestion in regard to greater expenditure is with respect to the research board. I believe they should be given every encouragement in the world to go ahead with projects which should be conducted for the benefit of our fisheries. During the past two years there has been considerable worry over the great decrease in the catch of sardines and herrings. If the canneries in Charlotte county had not been able to secure a supply of sardines from the state of Maine last year, not only the fishermen but the hundreds of people who work in the canneries would have been idle all summer. The same situation has existed this year. Eighty-five per cent

of the sardines being processed are being brought in from the state of Maine.
The minister referred to the importance of the herring investigation which is being carried out on the northeastern shores of our province, and he indicated that dead fish had been found on the ocean floor. This i3 a serious matter. Officials of the department have been investigating this problem and I hope they will be able to bring in a report which will be helpful. To my way of thinking this study should go on even for years if necessary, so they may come up with an answer which will be of value. I think it would be a good investment if the research board made a study of this branch of the industry, which covers the whole coast of New Brunswick, north, east, south and west. If an answer could be found as to why we have years of plenty and then two or three years with practically no herring at all, there would be great benefit to the industry. No one so far has been able to advise us or offer any suggestions as to why there cannot be a stable supply of this important fish which is in great demand.
Another suggestion I offer along these lines is that these surveys and studies would be much more helpful if they could be carried on internationally. I have always believed in international co-operation. Anything that affects our fisheries in the bay of Fundy also affects the fisheries along the Maine coast. The fisheries officials in that country have always been more than willing to co-operate and render any assistance possible, and this is one study which could be carried out in the two countries and prove most helpful. The sardine industry is a large industry in the state of Maine as well as in our part of this country.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings mentioned the Department of Transport regulations, which are bothering our fishermen to some extent. The statement the hon. member made is quite correct. I will say that the officials of the Department of Transport have been more than willing to try to adjust these differences. I should like to give one example to show what they have to contend with.
A lot of pressure is being put on to make it necessary to have a master's certificate in order to operate a boat of 10 tons or over. I have had a master's certificate for that particular type of boat, up to 150 tons, for a good many years. The examination for that certificate is not what one would call really tough. You must know the rules of the road, which should be known by anyone who

Supply-Fisheries
travels on the water. There are other regulations of which you must have knowledge, but the main thing is the eye test.
I know of young men down where I live who have been turned down completely because of their eyes. On one other occasion I stated on the floor of this house that those same persons could apply to drive a car in any province, and they would get a licence without any question whatever. Down there ladies and gentlemen of 75 years of age who must wear glasses are driving automobiles night and day in all kinds of weather without any thought that they might prove to be a hazard to traffic. But many young men in their thirties and forties, because their eyesight is not 100 per cent, are refused masters' certificates. That regulation, in so far as transport is concerned, is too rigid, or else our provincial regulations in connection with the granting of licences to drive motor cars are too easy.
The equipment they are obliged to have on board their boats is in many cases unreasonable. These men have spent their lives on salt water. They know exactly what they want for their own protection. One might say that in many cases they do not like to be told what they should have. If they have a dory with a pair of eight or nine-foot oars and the ordinary hardwood thole pins they are happy and, believe me, they will get ashore at times when it would scare anyone in this chamber. According to the regulations they have to have liferafts. If they purchased all the equipment the Department of Transport thinks they should have there would be very little room left in their boats for their fishing equipment.
I bring that to the attention of the minister because I believe it is a question of great importance and one that should be cleared up. These boats are manned by two or three men in most cases in my area. I want to say at this point that with regard to boats carrying passengers I have no criticism to offer about any regulations that are put into effect by the Department of Transport. If they are carrying passengers those passengers should be protected in every way. But the men who are going out to make a living with their own hands know what they need for their own protection. I believe their judgment in this respect would compare favourably with that of many who are trying to enforce the regulations today and make them carry further equipment.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings also mentioned export markets. Export markets mean so much to the fishing industry, particularly in the maritime provinces and, I would say, more particularly in

the area where I live because we are nearer the United States market. Everything possible should be done to keep those doors wide open. I appreciate the statement the minister made today in connection with the subsidy paid to the fisheries. It is true that the minute a subsidy is paid on a particular commodity, that commodity is barred from markets in the United States. It is felt that it would be unfair to allow a subsidized article to go into the United States competing with fishermen over there who are not subsidized, but those markets do mean so much to us.
Mention was made today of the scallop industry. This industry is carried on to a much greater extent in Nova Scotia than in the area where I live. I would hazard a guess that 85 per cent of the scallops produced in Nova Scotia are sold in the United States. There is another comparison I should like to put on the record. The Conley lobster company of St. Andrews, my own home town, are doing an enormous business. During the summer months they are shipping two or three refrigerator cars of live lobsters daily, besides the lobster meat they ship. I have the figures for 1953, but I do not have them for 1954. In 1953 over 96 per cent of the live lobsters and lobster meat sold by that company was sold in the United States. Less than 4 per cent was sold in Canada. When we depend on the American market to that extent, one should realize that we must do everything possible and use every argument possible to keep that market open to our fishermen.
There are several, I know, who wish to say a few words on these estimates, so there is just one other matter on which I shall touch before I resume my seat. I should like to congratulate the minister on the program he was able to work out with the Minister of Finance in connection with loans to fishermen. It is, I believe, legislation which will be of great benefit to good fishermen, men who really need assistance at times. This will get them over the hard spots. I hope it will be worked out in such a way that it will not be too complicated, and fishermen who can show that they are in a position to take care of their financial responsibilities will be given that assistance.
Unemployment insurance is a matter I shall not touch upon until later, when we get down to that item. With that I shall resume my seat. I shall ask some questions later on when the minister is replying, if he does, after the first item, as the result of a statement made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Would the minister put on the record, when he speaks, the size of the catch of Atlantic salmon for any one year

or two years, if possible? Could we have a comparison between the quantities caught commercially and the quantities caught by sports fishermen, and any figures he might have as to the decrease or increase in both catches?
Can he compare the quality?

I did not like to suggest the question of quality, because the minister would be well aware that Atlantic salmon is of much better quality than any salmon to be caught in any other parts of this country.

Mr. Chairman, in looking back over the past year with respect to the fisheries department, I think we can say that there has been a little more interest in fisheries generally in the House of Commons and at Ottawa. We had a discussion on the fisheries loans, and we also had some consideration of unemployment insurance for fishermen. There have also been the movies that have been shown by the department, and the fisheries dinners. While the fisheries committee has not been sitting, I suppose for obvious reasons-reasons that make it unnecessary for it to sit-we can say that generally there is a little better appreciation of and interest in the department.
I am perhaps a little more cynical and uncomplimentary than some of the other members. I think the trip of the minister to Russia is not perhaps going to mean a great benefit to the fisheries industry in Canada. It is hard to say that the fishermen generally are much better off than they were a year or two ago, but I shall say that there is an increasing feeling around the country, and here too, that the minister is showing to the department an attitude that is a little less temporary than that of previous ministers. In that respect he should be complimented, because that speaks well of the fisheries department. It may be that various internal cabinet shuffles mean that he cannot treat it in any other way, but this fact has been mentioned by many people and it is a good sign that the minister is considering his position in a little more permanent way than his predecessors have done.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say that in my own case I do not have the fisheries background of some of the members who have spoken, and I do not have day to day contacts with fishermen. I have to count on various articles and pamphlets that come out for most of my information. In this respect I find the Ftindy Fisherman, published at Blacks Harbour, very worth while. I also find the bulletins of the fisheries council of Canada very enjoyable reading, and
Supply-Fisheries
containing many good ideas. More particularly I should like to refer to a series of articles published in the Fredericton Gleaner written by Delbert Gallagher, a graduate student at the University of New Brunswick, who wrote some sort of a thesis on the fishing industry in New Brunswick. I do not know whether the very alert officials of the department have seen this. We do not have too much interest shown in this subject by our college students.
If I may, I should like to mention one or two of the points Mr. Gallagher brought out in this series of articles and in his thesis. First he refers to the fact that in the fishing industry, except for certain periods when we get abnormally high prices and when there are exceptionally good times in the good cycles, the rate of growth has always been behind that of other industries. He starts off by saying that fact must be recognized. He goes on with other points, and I have marked the points that I think are worthy of comment. He lays a great deal of blame on the fact that in the fisherman there is an inbred conservatism and individualism-that is conservatism with a small "c", I suppose, Mr. Chairman-and he presents the point of view that this fact goes to the root of the problem with which the fisherman himself is obliged to contend.
He then mentions the fact that in New Brunswick, and particularly down my way on the bay of Fundy, the part-time employment of fishermen is a problem and the fact that there is alternative employment is both a cause and effect; in other words, it is both good and bad. You have longshoremen and carpenters, etc., who take part in the fishing in Saint John harbour, for example, when the fish are running.
The problem presented in this. If they have good alternative occupations, what will be the effect of the fishing they do? In other words, if there are good alternative occupations they may forget all about fishing. On the other hand, if there are no other good occupations they may leave the area and forget about fishing entirely. That is a problem which must be faced, and it is well illustrated in this respect.
There is the matter of unions and organizations down our way, where there is smalltime fishing. The various fishermen-I refer to these part-time fishermen-have attempted to organize. They have had meetings and so on, but they have not got anywhere. There has been little success in that respect. I suppose we can say that where there are small-time fishermen like that there never will be good organization, and the benefits of union itself probably would not be too

Supply-Fisheries
great. These matters are mentioned. He mentions the industry itself. He mentions the monopoly that exists, but he also suggests that larger units are necessary in the fishing industry if we are to reap the benefits of marketing and the mass production that exists.
One problem that is well pointed out is this. When the fish are running and the large plants are operating, they tend to operate on a 10-hour day and so on, for various economic reasons. In consequence of this fact, and the fact that their production extends over just a short period, the fishermen who are counting on employment directly in the plants are left in the unfortunate position of having to do something else during the rest of the year. In other words, Mr. Chairman, I suppose there would never be the worry of the problem of a guaranteed annual wage for fishermen like these. It is simply absurd to suggest it when they have only two or three months' employment.
Before I leave this article I should like to say that it deals very well with the marketing problem. I imagine that most of the suggestions it makes are well understood by the department. However, if I may I should like to read a pertinent paragraph that commends itself to me:
Another major problem is consumer demand-* the trend has changed from the personal sale of the corner grocer to the impersonal business conducted by the freezers of the large food chain stores. Since most women buy on the impulse, the Canadian producer must pack his fish in attractive, space-saving and easy-to-open containers. If it is fresh fish, it should really be fresh. However, the basic point behind this is that producers should concentrate first on the domestic market and educate Canadians to eat fish and like it. Too long has fish been a Friday food; the time has come to bring it into the realms of respectability.
The minister referred to the fact that Canadians have a small fish consumption. This brief mentions that fact also. I leave that statement on marketing with the department.
Having reviewed this article I should just like to dwell on two matters which have not been touched upon and which, I will admit, have a local aspect as far as I am concerned. I refer first to the gaspereau fishing in the area of the Saint John harbour and Saint John river. There have been conflicting statements during the last two seasons. I know the department has investigated the matter quite extensively, but I feel that some definite statement should be made on the matter of gaspereau. One person has told the press that there has been trap net fishing in the spawning grounds at Grand lake. I understand that trap net fishing is not allowed in

the Saint John river, but that there has been trap net fishing at Grand lake and that it has depleted the stock. Another person has said

I believe it was one of the departmental officials-that the weather has been the great cause of the depletion. I feel that a complete investigation into this matter and a statement on it will help a great deal, because it is important to the fishermen in the area I represent.
Second, I refer to the salmon fishing in Saint John harbour and again in the river. The season started off slowly this year. While people are hopeful that the fishing will be much better as the season progresses, I call on the department to step up their research and investigation in connection with the salmon fishing in that area. We have always appreciated the fine salmon that are caught in Saint John harbour. A moment ago a question was asked, as to whether a comparison could be made with respect to various catches in the east and the west, and somebody interjected the question, could they compare the quality. This is an absurd statement, because everyone knows there is no comparison between the fine, pink, tasty, moist Saint John salmon and that pseudo salmon from the west.
You mean in the opinion of everybody from Saint John, New Brunswick.
