members themselves do not care enough to fight and ask for fresh fish.
Coming from the maritimes, I must admit that the meat dinners we get here are a decided treat to me, but I do not think I have had fish more than two or three times. When we had a fine dinner in the home economics kitchens of the fisheries department it brought home to me the fact that there is something wrong somewhere. I suggest that the solution lies in the hands of the members themselves.
It is a strange thing. Considering the fishing industry and comparing it with wheat, a product of the west, the fishermen work twice as hard for what they get, and certainly in depression times they feel the pinch far more than the western wheat growers. Yet there does not seem to be the interest. Here we have an industry that touches in some way practically all the provinces; at least, it affects all but two or three. The wheat industry is only concerned with two or three of the western provinces.
I leave that thought with the members here today, Mr. Chairman. We can talk about the department, we can talk about the research that is being done and we can try to get publicity all over the country, but a great deal of the responsibility falls upon the members themselves. I say we have to reassess our interests here and take a more active part in the consideration of this industry which produces this necessary food.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that in the present-day world there has been talk of going to the air in so far as our defence and our commercial life are concerned. We read of the various new plans that are being made and the increasing amount of money that is being spent on air activities. I do respect that, but I think it is fair to say also that in this atomic age, in our modern civilization, both Great Britain and the United States have realized that they have to get back to some extent to the sea and ships so far as defence purposes are concerned. I suggest very respectfully that we are also going to find it necessary to get back to the sea for our food.

The fisheries in Nova
Scotia and the Atlantic provinces generally are still our great undeveloped natural resource. The maritime people certainly cannot blame others. This resource has been with us for many generations and it is still in a retarded state of development. The western members have their prairies and as a result have developed a wheat industry. We maritimers have had, in the broad seas, a prairie at our doorsteps; yet we have failed

to fully develop its great wealth. I feel that the maritime people must accept the primary responsibility for the state of development of the fishing industry.
I know there have been certain historical and economic factors that have hindered the development of the industry in Nova Scotia and the other Atlantic provinces. But these historical and economic factors are not attributable either to our geographical location, or to a hostile government in Ottawa, or to any other factor, except factors with which the maritime people themselves should have coped earlier. I may say, however, they have been faced with increasing success in the past 10 years.
For the reason that this is an industry that we expect to develop and can develop by ourselves, I, in common with several hon. members, am very optimistic about the future development of the fisheries of Nova Scotia. As a matter of fact this is the only industry in my province that has shown signs of quickening life in the past number of years.
I agree with members who have pointed out the elements entering into the soundness of the fish industry, such as research, marketing, consumer education and so on. But the real ingredient necessary for further development in the fish industry is capital investment. As I pointed out when speaking at the resolution stage of the fishermen's loans bill, this capital investment must take place in the form of catching and processing equipment as well as in the field of distribution. At that time I mentioned that in 1939 the total investment in craft and gear in Nova Scotia amounted to $5,600,000, which represented a very small capital investment in the instruments with which the fisherman had to earn his living. I may say that in 1953 the total investment in craft and gear in Nova Scotia was something like $21 million, which represents a considerable improvement.
At the same time, it might be pointed out that the value of fishing craft in the Atlantic provinces, exclusive of Newfoundland, has increased by 175 per cent in the past 10 years, from $7-3 million to $203 million. The value of fishing gear has increased by about 120 per cent, from $6 million to $14-9 million. We have evidence here that there is a definite improvement in the capitalization of the fishing industry of Nova Scotia.
Despite the fact that the industry has been working in a favourable economic climate for the past 10 years, the capital investment has not been as great as we might have hoped. I would add that this increased investment in the industry in Nova Scotia has had a very direct bearing upon the physical productivity of the industry. In the pre-war

years the annual catch of fish in Nova Scotia ranged from 250 to 275 million pounds. It reached its high point in 1946, when it stood at 420 million pounds of fish. It now appears to be stabilized at about 380 million pounds. This increased poundage of fish landed certainly reflects the fact that there is a very close relationship between the capital invested in the industry and the physical productivity of the industry, and obviously therefore the return in the form of income to the fishermen.
The progress of the fishing industry on the Pacific coast has certainly been more rapid than that on the east coast. The value of fishing craft in the past 10 years on the Pacific coast has increased by 200 per cent. If you take into account the obvious adjustments that have to be made for changes in prices, the per man investment on the Pacific coast has doubled in that period. This is reflected in the greater size of the boats, better equipment and better devices for locating fish. We in the maritime provinces still have to catch up in this very important and crucial part of the industry if we are to provide the equipment and the gear that is essential in pursuing this occupation.
In the field of processing, in the past 10 years the number of plants in the maritime provinces has increased and the number of plant workers has decreased, showing greater mechanization. The same trend is shown on the Pacific coast. We have evidence, therefore, that in the field of processing, investment is also occurring. In the field of distribution, investment has been very slow, because there is no real way to attack this problem of providing necessary investment in refrigeration and fish display, those things which are so essential if we are to attract and satisfy the central Canadian consumer of fish. It is difficult to outline clearly how direction can be given to this form of investment, but it goes without saying that this investment is very essential in the stores and groceterias across the country if we are to provide refrigerated fresh products to the central Canadian consumer.
I have mentioned the development of investment and an increase in the landings of fish both in Nova Scotia and on the Pacific coast. I must say that this has not been exclusively the result of a new lease on life on the part of fishermen or businessmen in the industry, but has been the result of a favourable economic climate under which the fishing industry has been operating for the last 10 years. Anyone who will look at the wholesale price index for fish products for the past 20 years will find there has been a very great increase in wholesale fish prices.

If we take the period 1935-39 as the base of 100, we find that in 1945 the index stood at 270. During the same time the increase in the consumer price index has been much less. So the fishing industry, and fishermen, have been working in this desirable economic climate for the last number of years. To a great extent that has accounted for increased investment, physical productivity and income of fishermen.
Already several members have referred to the importance of markets, particularly to the importance of cultivating the domestic market and increasing the per capita consumption of fish in Canada. It should be remembered that the Canadian consumer still exercises freedom of choice, and chooses among products on the basis of price and consumer tastes. If the domestic market for fish is to be properly developed, and extended in Canada, it involves first of all the type of investment which will provide facilities by way of refrigeration and display, and also the type of advertising that will induce the Canadian consumer to buy more fish.
Indeed, we have certain natural attractions in connection with fish that should recommend themselves to Canadian consumers. Fish is one of the best protein foods; with proper development in the industry it should have a wider and ever-growing market on the Canadian domestic scene.
I agree with all the sentiments that have been expressed about the necessity of extending the sale of Canadian fish in the United States market. I would mention, however, that the New England fisheries, which represent the real pressure group for increased protection for the United States product, have been facing very great difficulties. The number of fishermen and the number of boats engaged in this industry are quickly diminishing, as a result of the operation of the definite competitive advantage of our Atlantic producers. The distance from the fishing banks and the higher wage levels in the New England fisheries have brought about the great competitive advantage held by our producers. I am reasonably optimistic on this point, that for some time there will be a desire on the part of United States public men, and indeed the industry itself, to moderate the effect of these competitive advantages so the decline in the industry will not be too rapid.
Indeed, Senator Kennedy of Massachusetts has suggested protection, not to maintain the New England fisheries permanently at present levels, but rather to modify the rather difficult readjustment that would be involved by a sudden elimination of this industry. I am reasonably optimistic that the future will see

Supply-Fisheries
the gradual elimination of the New England fisheries because of the competitive advantage held by our Atlantic producers, and the greater possibility of the sale of our product in the great United States market.
I might suggest that in our discussion of the fishing industry we should not overemphasize ground fisheries. I believe they deserve all the emphasis they get, but the ground fisheries sometimes can be overemphasized at the expense of other forms of sea food. For example, lobster is still our most valuable single species of fish in my part of the world. The catch of lobsters cannot be centralized. You have to depend on the catch along the coast line in many communities in the maritime provinces. If we intend to catch this valuable product of the sea, then we must see to it that the people in the coastal villages who take the lobsters from the sea are given a proper standard of living. From this point of view the Department of Fisheries should be interested not only in the economic aspects of the lobster fisheries but also the social aspects in those villages along the coast line of the maritime provinces, where this type of fisherman lives. It is very essential that he be provided with a proper standard of living.
I might say in conclusion that of equal importance to the economic factors that have affected the fishing industry in the maritime provinces has been the influence of certain individuals in that industry who have exerted considerable force in the thinking of the industry. I would refer first of all to the former deputy minister of fisheries, whose analysis of the industry and whose leadership in it have been of well recognized value.
This past winter the united maritime fishermen celebrated their 25th anniversary. It is an organization composed principally of inshore fishermen of the maritime provinces. The organization grew out of a royal commission appointed in 1928 to investigate the fishing industry of the maritimes. One of the recommendations of that commission was that a program of education and organization should be undertaken among the fishermen of the maritime provinces. To achieve that very difficult and toilsome task the government appointed Dr. M. M. Coady, who later founded the extension department at Anti-gonish, and who has since laboured constantly in the interests of the fishermen of the Atlantic provinces. Because Dr. Coady has done such outstanding work, and because he is now retired from the active direction of the extension department I felt I should link his name with that of Stewart Bates as among
[Mr. MacEachen.l
the men who have wielded great influence in the development of the fisheries in my part of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on this first item. At this time last year I was not a member of the House of Commons, but I made it my business to read Hansard of the time the minister's estimates were before the house. I have always been impressed by the way the minister handles his estimates. When he finishes his remarks on the first item he has generally cleared up many of the questions that no doubt are in the minds of different hon. members. In his statement last year the minister said, as reported on page 4499 of Hansard of May 7, 1954:
. . . by just touching briefly on the division of jurisdiction between the federal Department of Fisheries and the provincial departments of fisheries because there is some doubt in some members' minds about that point. Under our constitution the federal government has complete jurisdiction over fisheries, but over the years we have worked out with the provinces what is a very satisfactory arrangement under which they usually administer sport fisheries, which are of course of primary value to them in recreation and the tourist trade, and we handle the commercial fisheries, especially those of the two coasts. The federal government pass all regulations concerning fisheries, even for the sport fisheries of the provinces, and of course do the research work, and the inspection of fish for interprovincial trade or for export.
That statement cleared up many of the things about which I was in doubt at the time. I have listened to hon. members who have preceded me tell about salmon on one coast or salmon on the other, but I am ready to let them keep their salmon as long as I can get Winnipeg goldeye, Winnipeg whitefish and a bit of pickerel for a change. Coming from the prairies as I do I am naturally interested in the fishing industry of Manitoba. 1 know that Manitoba looks after her own commercial fisheries as well as her own sports fisheries. I realize that there is a great deal of cooperation between the federal and provincial governments, but at this time I should like to appeal for still greater co-operation.
I feel that we in Manitoba are missing the boat by not being able to participate in the different activities sponsored by the federal government and paid for out of the consolidated revenue. When we were in difficulties some time ago in selling our surplus fish, we had the co-operation of the federal government in disposing of it. In the estimates this year there is an item of $80,000 for cooperative education among fishermen. In the past advantage has been taken of this vote by fishermen on both east and west coasts. I understand that the Department of Fisheries

has gone even further and is introducing a scheme to educate young men to be better fishermen than their fathers were before them. I appeal to the Minister of Fisheries and also to the minister in Manitoba responsible for the fishing industry for closer cooperation so the fishermen on lake Manitoba and lake Winnipeg can participate and have the advantage of this educational program the federal government is paying for.
This $80,000 comes out of the dominion treasury and is to be used by the fishing industry for co-operative education in buying and selling fish. Further co-operation would no doubt bring us under the fishermen's indemnity fund, which is a scheme of insurance provided by the federal government for their boats. I know that today no fishermen on either lake Winnipeg or lake Manitoba are able to get insurance at the rate of 1 per cent which is charged on the insurance provided to fishermen by the dominion government. It is true that insurance is provided for only 60 per cent of the value of a boat, up to $7,500.
Coming back to the money voted for educational work and the training of young fishermen, may I say that I should like to see some of this money spent in Manitoba for this purpose. The fishermen's indemnity fund is a good thing and should be available to all fishermen who have boats, either large or small. I have not before me at the present time the insurance rates applicable for lake Winnipeg, but I have no doubt they are much more than the 1 per cent, which is the rate fishermen pay under the fishermen's indemnity fund. I should like to see Manitoba fishermen have the opportunity of participating in both these schemes, that is the educational plan and the fishermen's indemnity fund for the insurance of boats. I ask the minister for his co-operation along with that of the minister responsible in Manitoba in order that these two projects, which are so valuable, may be made available to our fishermen.
The work being done by the department in connection with the control of pests such as the lamprey in the large eastern lakes is both interesting and educational. As a member of the marine and fisheries committee I had the pleasure of seeing the film which was produced, and I think the government and the department should be congratulated. I hope money can be found with which to produce other films like that, because such films educate a person much more quickly than anything he might read.
I should like at this time to congratulate the fisheries council of Canada upon their biweekly bulletin. This contains considerable
Supply-Fisheries
condensed information, it is easy reading, and no paper is wasted as it is printed on both sides. I welcome the fisherman's loan act, which perhaps I should not speak about at this time, and I do hope that when this legislation is passed it will apply to prairie fishermen.
In closing I would extend a hearty invitation to the minister to visit Manitoba's inland port of Selkirk and see not only the up to date fishing plants of the various fish packing companies but the fishing boats and the men who earn their livelihood in the fishing industry.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with special interest this morning to the statement of the Minister of Fisheries on the activities of his department. It was gratifying and encouraging to hear from the minister that the catch and market situation had improved substantially during the past year and that prospects for the present season are promising. In the course of his remarks the minister covered in interesting and instructive detail the activities of his department and of most of its different services. I want to join with hon. members who have spoken before me in congratulating the minister upon his masterful presentation.
We all recognize that one of the main responsibilities of the Department of Fisheries is to help maintain and develop fish stocks in Canadian inland and coastal waters in order to protect the annual returns to the industry. As representatives in this house of the Canadian people we must not disregard our responsibility toward the immense fishing resources of our country, which are contributing substantially to our general economy. We must recognize that the possible expansion of our fisheries is still of paramount importance to our coastal provinces, and rightly deserves the special attention of the Canadian parliament. After all, the abundant marine life of the Atlantic coast of North America has been one of the main factors in leading Europeans to their first contact with our continent. The teeming waters of the Atlantic are yielding today, it is true, owing to improved fishing methods and greater catching efficiency, perhaps almost as freely as in the days of Cabot, and are instrumental in the growth of this important primary industry.
In the course of my remarks during the fisheries estimates debate last year I stressed the urgent need for an educational program and a well prepared publicity campaign to prevent the unfortunate practice of illegal fishing, too common among a large number of our fishermen, mainly in lobster fishing.

Supply-Fisheries
I want to express my appreciation for the preliminary action taken by the minister and his department in this respect. I wish to assure the minister that the series of lectures and conferences undertaken in the summer of 1954 and carried on earlier this year at the lobster fishing centres of new Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have been most beneficial.
I was given the opportunity of being present at one of these meetings, which was held at Sacred Heart University at Bathurst on November 26 last, and which was attended by well over 600 persons from all sections of northeastern New Brunswick. I wish to congratulate Dr. Wilder of the St. Andrews biological station, who was in charge of those lectures or conferences. I wish to assure the minister that we are looking forward to a continuation and expansion of this educational policy.
It is most unfortunate, however, that the fisheries research board is not in a position to provide the services of a man conversant with French, which is the sole language of at least 85 per cent of the fishermen in the counties of Westmorland, Kent, Northumberland and Gloucester. If pamphlets describing the life and habits of the lobster, such as those distributed by Dr. Wilder in the course of his lectures, were made available to school children in lobster fishing centres, the effect, I am convinced, would be most beneficial.
On Tuesday evening the members of the marine and fisheries committee were given the privilege of attending the premiere of a film describing a lobster fishing operation as carried on by commercial lobster fishermen. This was followed by two short films or scripts, one on lobster conservation and the other on the factors affecting the lobster catch. These films were well prepared, and the national film board as well as the Department of Fisheries deserve to be congratulated for this most interesting and educational accomplishment. I sincerely hope the school children in lobster fishing centres will be given the opportunity to see those educational films, and that French versions will be provided in localities where the French language is predominant.
In looking over the fisheries estimates for the fiscal year 1955-56 I note a proposed decreased expenditure of $344,211. It does not seem in line with the principles of good business that a department concerned with a growing and expanding industry such as fisheries should be asked to curtail its budget and cut down expenditures. I note, however, with some satisfaction that the amount to be voted for the fisheries research board shows

an increase of $309,000. This is a step in the right direction, but this item is by far too low if we are to take into consideration the great potentialities and the needs of the fishing industry.
At the main entrance of the parliament buildings are engraved the following words, which have been quoted on different occasions on the floor of this house: "The wholesome sea is at her gates, her gates both east and west". This wholesome sea offers the largest variety of fish products in the world, and Canada today is the world's leading exporter of this particular commodity. It was encouraging to hear the minister state that in 1954 Canadian fisheries exports had increased by 17 per cent.
The fishing industry, Mr. Chairman, which is also an industry whose successes or failures depend on natural causes and are subject to the elements of nature, in the past has been called upon to assume the major share of responsibility for its subsistence. Up to March 31, 1953, the agricultural prices support board showed a net cost of operation amounting to over $42 million. Just a few weeks ago the Minister of Agriculture informed this house that recent payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to 21,000 farmers in Manitoba amounted to close to $4 million, while those paid to 85,000 farmers in Saskatchewan totalled $20 million, representing in this case over 75 per cent of all the farmers of that particular province.
It is true that the fisheries prices support board, in existence since 1947, has cost the government of this country slightly over $4 million. However, the deep-sea fishermen of my province and of the Gaspe coast experienced in 1952 one of the most disastrous seasons since the end of the second world war. It has taken the two full fishing seasons of 1953 and 1954 for a large number of these fishermen to pay back the debts assumed during 1952. Their numerous appeals to the fisheries prices support board did not receive favourable consideration.
The minister explained this morning the reasons for the board's decision in this particular case. Fortunately the market situation gradually improved in 1953, but the fact still remains that thousands of fishermen had to assume the full responsibility for a most unfavourable fishing season followed by a declining market. The minister's announcement that the department would pay 50 per cent of the cost of salt used in processing some of the varieties of fish will be welcomed in the areas where fishermen are curing their own fish. It will, however, have very little effect in the province of New Brunswick.

A few weeks ago I brought to the attention of the minister a serious epidemic decimating herring in the bay of Chaleur and the gulf of St. Lawrence. Here again hundreds of herring fishermen had to bring home their nets and fishing gear after a most unsuccessful season. The lobster fishermen of this particular area are seriously affected, and in the short, two-month season of May and June a large number will not land enough lobsters to meet the heavy expenses of traps, rope and other fishing gear and equipment required to carry on their operations.
I realize the importance of agriculture, and particularly of wheat, to the general economy of this country. It is gratifying to us from the maritime provinces to hear the word "fish" added to this echo of wheat, box cars and more wheat which originates almost daily from the floor of this house, and is repeated on practically every page of Hansard. If it rains too much, we hear this plea for assistance. If we have a drought period, help is asked for. If the crop is below normal, the government is pressed for a bonus or a grant. If there is overproduction the great benefactor, this benevolent institution known as the federal government, is called upon to come to the rescue and find a market in which to dispose of this surplus crop. The poor hard-working fisherman, in the meantime, must face practically alone the hazards of the weather and the sea, and stand on his own whether or not he brings home the harvest from the ocean.
Mr. Chairman, I insist that increased fisheries research is necessary if the industry is to prosper and if the intensive export of fisheries resources is to be maintained without endangering the abundant supply of our diversified fish species. One must not neglect the importance of biological data which are today, if not almost lacking, certainly much too limited on such common varieties of fish as cod, flounder, haddock, herring and other species found in abundance in our Atlantic waters.
I should like to mention at this time the Atlantic herring investigation committee which was operated for a number of years as a joint effort of the governments of Canada and Newfoundland-this was before Newfoundland entered confederation-and the provincial governments of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Hydrographic studies were made of the herring life, and the knowledge of conditions in the gulf area was substantially increased. This committee, I understand, was dissolved in 1949 or 1950. The fisheries research board has been carrying on the investigation since then. A period of five years,
Supply-Fisheries
however, has elapsed and we are still waiting for the report of the results or findings of this most useful study.
In the meantime, in most of the fishing centres of the maritime provinces our herring fishermen are still using the same outmoded and inefficient methods adopted by their forefathers over a century ago. The lack of information concerning such an important species is astonishing, and improvement can be obtained only by an expanding research program and by the application to the industry of all available technical and biological knowledge.
In this respect, Mr. Chairman, we are all interested in receiving at the earliest possible date the full findings of the Atlantic herring investigation committee which, I understand, operated for a period of five or six years. Such a report would be of valuable assistance to our herring fishermen.
It is not my intention to minimize the importance of and the good work accomplished by the fisheries research board. However, the activities of this board are limited by restricted funds. As a result, our fishing industry is not getting the full benefit of the resources of modern science applicable to this particular field. As we all know, and as the minister stated this morning, our fishermen are handicapped by an invisible drifting of sea pasturage and a continuous migration of fish. The best knowledge of modern science is required if the effects of the shifting tides and currents are to be mastered and controlled. The sea offers an unexplored frontier of possibilities for our scientists, and our men having chemical and biological skill must be provided with the facilities required if we want mankind to benefit from these untapped treasures of the ocean. We are depending on the Minister of Fisheries to press the government to enlarge by all means the scope of the fisheries research board and, whenever possible, to make its results and findings better known and applicable in a more practical way to the common commercial fishermen, especially on the Atlantic coast.
A few years ago we had a growing and productive oyster industry on the north shore of New Brunswick. In 1949 the oyster crop in New Brunswick reached a peak production of 37,000 barrels. In 1950 it was down to 26,000 barrels and has been decreasing ever since. The last statistical report for 1954 shows a total landing of less than 12,000 barrels, or one-third of the 1949 production. Mr. Chairman, with New Westminster having such a vital interest in the fishing business I am satisfied that it is most important that I should have something to say in this debate. A year ago I had occasion to compliment the minister on the reconsideration of the problem with respect to the closure of fishing above Pattullo bridge. Today I listened with considerable interest to what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert had to say with respect to the minister's reason for doing such a good job with the fisheries, and I am afraid I cannot agree with him. I must be fair and say that I think the minister found a certain challenge in the fisheries department and decided to do something about it. Knowing the Minister of Fisheries as we on the Pacific coast do, rightly or wrongly you can expect that he will do something about it.
In the instance to which I referred I considered that he was wrong in his decision, and I cannot quite understand why he has not made reference to the closure of that fishing in this debate. I must therefore accept my own thought that he contemplates no change. I spoke on this question in the house on two occasions, and the minister was present on at least one. I see no reason to restate what I said on those occasions. He is fully aware how the fishermen on the Fraser river feel about this matter. The hon. member for Fraser Valley has also indicated how the fishermen in his area dislike the continuance of the closure. However, I have certain questions I should like to place before the minister with respect to this matter, and if he will answer them it may help us in some way to understand his point of view and the reasons for the closure.
In the course of his remarks this morning the minister mentioned the need for a pink salmon treaty, and he was kind enough to say that I was present at the meeting that was held. I am satisfied that something should and must be done as quickly as possible in this regard. He did say that this year the fishermen are stepping out and trying to out-fish the Americans in order to prove that we can practically force them to come to some agreement. This was indicated at the meeting, as the minister has been given to understand, and the fishermen's unions on either side of the international boundary came to a tentative agreement that they wanted their governments to do something about the matter.
Supply-Fisheries
More particularly the suggestion has been made by the fishermen, myself and others that the present sockeye salmon commission might be utilized for this purpose. Being as familiar as they are with sockeye salmon and the salmon industry as a whole, we feel that they might do an excellent job if they were also given jurisdiction over pink salmon.
One question I have has to do with catches of pink salmon. From 1933 to 1953-I do not have the 1954 catch here-the minister said the catch was on about a 40-60 basis. I believe the figures are derived from the pack figures, using an average of 12 to a case, which would indicate that in 1953 Canada caught somewhat over 4 million pink salmon and the United States 6J million, or a total of over 10J million. That would be about a 40-60 split. Actually it works out at approximately 38 per cent as far as Canada is concerned.
However, in 1941 Canadian fishermen caught 1,400,000 pink salmon and the Americans only caught 2 million, a total catch of 3,400,000. In that year Canada had about 41 per cent of the catch. Possibly the war had something to do with it, but if the minister would explain the difference and the reason for our trying to outfish the Americans it might be of interest to the fishermen. In 1951 we caught approximately 35 per cent. We caught 2,895,000 compared with 5,300,000 caught by the Americans, or a total of 8,195,000. The 35 per cent is not very far below the 38 per cent, and we did that without out-fishing the Americans.
I am not going to suggest for a moment that we should not try to outfish the Americans. I think we should. I think his plan of trying to bring them to terms is excellent, and I am satisfied that the fishermen in my area feel likewise. I should like to compliment him on instituting the program of trying to outfish the Americans with the full intention of making them realize that there is only one practical way of preserving the pink salmon-by mutual agreement-possibly on a 50-50 basis similar to what obtain in the sockeye salmon industry.
Then I have certain other questions. How have the Fraser valley fishermen failed in their attempt to conserve salmon in the past? Would he not agree that the fact they caught more salmon last year than in any other year was the result of these fishermen conserving salmon in former years and co-operating in every way, shape and form with the minister and the officials of his department who make the regulations? I feel satisfied that was done; therefore it is rather difficult for me, as it must be for the fishermen, to understand why there is need for this change if conservation is the point.

Supply-Fisheries
If it is not conservation, then it must be quality. On a percentage basis, from what fishing grounds were the greatest number of fish lost due to spoilage? I know our gill net fishermen are outfished in the straits and up the inlet, but on a percentage basis from what grounds do the fish come that are lost through spoilage? Are they from the seine vessels or from the gill netters? In this regard let us take the past three or four years. I am not interested in going further back, although I am satisfied that the same results would be obtained.
How are the regulations enforced regarding seiners fishing off the lightship in the Fraser river? The gill net vessel owners fishing downstream from the Pattullo bridge inform me that seiners come right up to within a few yards of the lightship, and the understanding is that they should be something like ten miles away from there. How are these regulations enforced to ensure that this does not happen?
Another question which actually requires the co-operation of the veterans affairs department is what compensation, if any, is being considered for the war veterans who settled above the Pattullo bridge who were given a licence to fish in that area? I understand they are now to be denied that licence, and I wondered what compensation they were to receive for being deprived of these particular fishing grounds.
I have one or two other observations to make with respect to the debate that has taken place. In so far as the marketing of our product is concerned, I would agree with those who have indicated that possibly the most important market for our fisheries industry is the home market. During a recent trip to my home I was very pleased to find one of the dining cars serving Pacific coast salmon. I was more than pleased to find that it was prepared to perfection; even the hon. member for Fraser Valley would have approved. Apparently the chef did an excellent job. Word very soon got around the dining car, and people were ordering salmon. Ordinarily we find that when word gets around that fish is not prepared as well as it might be the result is that this product does not get its share of the consumer market. This incident proved to me that when fish is well prepared there will be a demand for it.
I would go along with the idea of including a chef's course or something similar in the course the minister indicated is being offered by the University of British Columbia. When the minister was speaking I wondered whether or not this course would be available to summer students. I see he is shaking his head

to indicate that it is not. It is unfortunate that it is not. Possibly the university will see fit to broaden the course and make it available to summer students as well. Frequently we find people who are anxious to learn these things who would like to take summer courses.
I should like to make one other suggestion. Actually I might refer to what I said last year during one of the debates on the tourist industry. At that time I suggested that instead of Canadian restaurants advertising southern fried chicken we should have a Canadian dish. It might be a provincial dish, and encouragement of this idea might be given by our fisheries department. The department might suggest that restaurants advertise such things as barbecued salmon, Winnipeg gold-eye or whatever dish might be appropriate in the various provinces. Those of us who have long distances to travel find that from time to time the steward on the train comes to us and suggests that a certain fish is available; it has just been freshly brought in. We should not be dependent upon the ability of the steward alone to sell that commodity.
Of course, a great deal depends upon the preparation. It would really be a fine thing if tourists from the United States and other lands could come to Canada and be assured that the fish they obtain in the restaurants is not only of the best quality but prepared to perfection, and that it is a national dish.
I shall say no more at this time. I hope the minister answers these questions, and I may have others to put to him, depending upon what he has to say.

I should like to add my congratulations, Mr. Chairman, to those that have already been given the Minister of Fisheries upon his opening remarks in presenting the estimates of his department to this committee. I want to say a few words on behalf of the fishermen of Newfoundland, in connection with the announcement that the government has decided to pay 50 per cent of the cost of salt used in the making of salt codfish. I feel sure that this announcement will be greatly appreciated by them. It will be the means of putting some heart into them as they are about to start the fishing operations for 1955.
Last year we were blessed by Providence with a large catch of cod. As the minister said, the fish that came in were almost eating the rocks and they were the means of providing the fishermen with the necessities of life. While I do not want to take very much of the time of the committee, I should like to say that we in Newfoundland have our problems. I hope, however, that we shall

be able to make a great contribution to Canada. We have great resources in Newfoundland, and when those resources are developed they will be of great assistance to the dominion as a whole. This is my hope.
The provision for payment of 50 per cent of the cost of the salt used by fishermen will, I hope, enable fishermen to produce larger quantities of salt cod. According to the latest report it would appear that Norway and Iceland will produce as much salt codfish this year as last year, or perhaps more. There is no reason to assume that the fleets from Spain, Portugal and France that fish off the Grand Banks will get any less fish than they did last year. Because of their great mobility, they can move from the Grand Banks to Greenland and get additional catches when completing their trip.
However, I understand that the sales of salt cod in Europe this year are not less than those of last year, and may be slightly higher. It is my hope that Newfoundland will be able to enter the European salt cod markets. It is too bad that in the past we have not been able to participate in this market, because our customers over there are producing their own fish and naturally the market is more restricted. We have been practically eliminated from the Brazilian market, which in the past took large quantities of Newfoundland salt cod. This has been the result of currency restrictions and perhaps a lowering of internal purchasing power. In Newfoundland we find we have not been able to sell as much salt cod to Brazil as we did formerly.
I hope we will be able to enter this European market. At the moment Iceland sells a great deal of salt cod in Europe. It seems that the quality of our salt cod, whether it is on account of the longer ocean voyage or for some other reason, does not stand up as well as that of the Iceland cod. I think steps should be taken to ascertain the cause of that, to find out why the meat of the fish seems to disintegrate a bit more than the fish from Iceland.
We are told that our stock position is favourable. I hope the catch this year will be plentiful for our fishermen. Of course that depends to a great extent upon currents and winds and the way the fish travel. We know they are always in search of food and, as I said before, a good deal will depend upon the amount of food available in the form of the smaller fish such as caplin, to attract them inshore.
We in Newfoundland have to face the problem of looking after trap fishing. In the last two or three years we have had good trap
Supply-Fisheries
fishing. After all, it is one of the cheapest ways of producing fish, that of catching them in traps. The fishermen put out their traps. The fish come in conveniently near the traps, run along the leaders and by and by are found in the traps. It is simply a matter of closing the mouth of the trap, hauling it in and taking out the fish. However, this naturally depends upon the fish coming in to shore.
No doubt there will be a time when the fish will not come in so near the shore, and we will have to look into the matter of going out after them. This suggests the idea of providing long-liners to fishermen to go out and use trawls to get the fish on the grounds where they are located. In this connection I was glad to hear the minister this morning speak about the progress that has been made in connection with the mapping of the grounds and new banks. When he is summing up I would ask him to tell us what steps have been taken to place that information in the hands of fishermen in the different localities, because such information is very valuable. They should know where the new grounds are located.
We know conservation is very important. Mention has already been made this afternoon of the film shown the other evening about lobster fishing. The Department of Fisheries is to be congratulated on that excellent film; and I feel sure that as it is shown throughout Canada it will increase knowledge, a factor which is very necessary for those who must deal with the problem of conserving the lobster fisheries.
Loans for primary producers is a move in the right direction; and I hope it will be only a matter of time when some form of unemployment insurance will be provided for our fishermen.
Today the minister spoke about seals. Over 30 years ago I went out and caught some seals. I left in the morning before daylight carrying a gaff over my shoulder. I had my hauling line and was wearing a pair of sealskin boots. One thing I remember about the experience was that I had to wring out my socks several times before I got back that day, and was assisted to shore by the foghorn which was blowing from the top of Long Point, and which we heard as we were coming in a mile or a mile and a half offshore.
These seals are very important. I think the question of whether or not the Norwegian ships that come out here to take part in the seal fishery are being subsidized should be inquired into. When I went seal fishing the practice was to carry the gaff over one shoulder, and to stun the seal. I remember

Supply-Fisheries
killing three young hoods. I took my gaff, struck them over the head, stunned them and then of course got out my knife and took out the carcass. I hauled them in with my hauling rope. I understand that last winter even some of the women in Newfoundland went to the seal fishery. I know of one case where a search party had to go out during the evening with flashlights to assist the women to get in with their seals. This is a very important industry, and I think we should look after it as well as possible.
Then I would bring to the attention of the minister the quality of codfish. If possible something should be done to encourage people to make the best quality of codfish. I do not know whether anything can be done by way of bonuses or extra payments to encourage the making of good codfish; but something should be done, because we certainly do not want to lose that art. We know that in many industries rapid technical progress is being made, and we are looking forward to this progress being extended to the fishing industry.
We know that artificial driers are a great help to fishermen. In the past they had to depend upon the sun, and their own efforts and those of their wives and families, to spread the fish on the flakes so they would be dried and available for market. Ample funds should be provided so the work of the research board will proceed at the maximum speed possible.
I see it is about two minutes to six, and I shall have time to refer to one further matter. I have the honour to represent Labrador, with a very extensive coast line. Let me say in passing that since confederation only one wharf has been built on the whole of the Labrador coast line. I realize that this does not come under the minister's department, but the fact remains that the fishermen do need wharves. While there are not many fishermen on the extended coast line, they do need certain facilities in the different localities, the fishing settlements and outports in which they live. We look forward to the time when the Department of Public Works will provide these facilities.
There is one further matter concerning Labrador, and that is the very important salmon fishery. Salmon, which at the present time bring in about three or four dollars each, will in time become very valuable. In fact I would not be at all surprised-perhaps not in my time, but later-the time will come when every salmon will be worth perhaps $100. I know there are Americans who go to the Labrador coast now and who are prepared to invest large sums of money in fishing gear, lines, reels and all that sort of thing

in order to engage in this sports fishing. I would ask the minister to see that an additional sum of money is provided so that additional salmon guardians may be provided in Labrador.
There is one other matter I should like the minister to deal with when he speaks by and by, and that is to give a review of the industrial development with regard to Newfoundland.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the first item of this department's estimates, as I come from a province where fishing is the second most important industry. In the province of Prince Edward Island the annual catch is in the neighbourhood of 30 million pounds, and its landed value is something over $3 million, with the market value in the neighbourhood of $4 million.
I note with interest that the fishing industry is gradually assuming its rightful place of importance, with improved legislation being put on the statute books from time to time. I am especially pleased to see that at last action has been taken to provide medium-term loans for fishermen, as have been available for agriculture for some time. The Department of Fisheries, of course, in addition to its prime function, is also responsible for various boards and other organizations such as the fisheries research board, the fishermen's indemnity fund, the fisheries prices support board and a number of other such bodies which come under the minister's department.
I have read with interest the reports of these various boards. On reading the annual report of the fisheries prices support board I came upon two small items, both of which interested me. Perhaps the minister would be kind enough to explain them at some suitable time. On page 11 I notice that expenditures for the year 1953-54 include the sum of $6.45 for postage, which seems a relatively small amount, and the sum of $631.39 for telephones and telegrams. It would appear on the face of it that the board finds it necessary to carry on most of its communication by either telegram or telephone. Of course that may not be the true explanation. I noticed too, on page 5, a statement which struck me as being especially curious-this in a lighter vein-since the minister himself

is a Rhodes scholar. I see what appears to be a piece of rather poor construction. It says in part:
In 1953 the fishery on the west coast returned to generally normal levels of production while the Atlantic fishermen, influenced by biological and economic factors which in some instances discouraged fishing effort and lowered productivity, took from the waters a reduced yield.
I take it that the biological factors were operating on the fish rather than on the fishermen; but that is just in passing. Although the Department of Fisheries is fairly extensive, I note with interest that all the activities of the federal government having to do with fisheries are not contained in this department. Of course that may be unavoidable. But I notice that the report of the national parks branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources gives over almost a whole page to fisheries studies of various kinds which that department carries out. I would be interested to know what liaison there is between the two departments. I assume it is very close, and I assume that this work in the parks branch refers only to fish in waters within the boundaries of national parks.
In my province of Prince Edward Island the coastal fisheries, especially the lobster fishery, are of prime importance. Although dragging is now becoming important and there is a very healthy industry building up in that field, nevertheless the lobster fishery is, as yet at any rate, the most important. Here is something I should like to bring to the minister's attention. I know it does not directly concern his department; nevertheless it has to do with the welfare of the fishermen and the circumstances under which they operate.
In former years there was a very considerable coastal trade in the maritimes. As a result the Department of Public Works saw fit to provide small wharves in almost all the little coves around the maritimes. In many cases now that the coastal trade has practically disappeared, owing in the first place to the railways and then to trucking, these wharves have fallen into disrepair or have become non-existent. At the present time almost the only purpose for which these wharves would be used would be for the accommodation of local fishermen. The result is that there are many cases where wharves or shelters for fishing boats are not provided. There may be cases where wharves are provided for a now extinct coastal trade. Such wharves are no longer necessary.
I would suggest that some means of close liaison be developed between the Department of Fisheries and the Department of
Supply-Fisheries
Public Works so that recommendations could be made by the Department of Fisheries as to where expenditures should be made to provide shelters for fishing boats. I think the department should be in a better position to make such recommendations than any smaller group or any individuals, because if you have individuals making recommendations, or even small groups you have the question of local pride and the procedure of trying to establish something that may not be justified in one case but may be highly justified in another.
For example, in my own riding I know there are certain areas, especially on the north shore, where the fishermen operate under most severe difficulties. There are places where a number of fishing boats operate and where the fishermen have no adequate shelter for the boats at all. They are obliged to be on the watch all the time and if a storm comes up drag their boats out of the water by means of horses or some other means.
Having said that, I should like to turn for a few moments to the fresh water fisheries of Prince Edward Island. They are not of any direct economic importance, but they are a great tourist attraction. In most provinces I presume that much of the angling is done within the boundaries of the national or provincial parks, but in the case of Prince Edward Island the most attractive angling areas are on private property or, in any case, outside the boundaries of the national park.
I was interested to read in the Canada Year Book of 1952-53 a paragraph which refers to this particular problem in Prince Edward Island. Perhaps I shall be pardoned if I quote it just to refresh the minister's memory on the problem. It is to be found at page 577:
The streams of the province-
This is referring to Prince Edward Island. -are, as a whole, mostly spring fed and fairly constant in flow, thus providing excellent spawning grounds and nurseries for game fish, of which speckled trout are by far the most important. With such favourable conditions for reproduction the problem is to increase the production of trout of a size attractive to anglers. Comprehensive biological investigations are being carried on by the fisheries research board to attain this objective by determining the most efficient procedure in stocking, managing and cropping. The province provides the sites for these investigations and the conservation and development branch of the federal Department of Fisheries builds the necessary dams and supplies the fish required for experimental purposes.
The angling pressure in this province is continuing to increase but many of the fertile and highly productive ponds have disappeared. During 1951, the department, with a view to readjusting this situation, has repaired dams and restored

Supply-Fisheries
many pends and thus opened to the public, subject to the prevailing fishery regulations, many angling areas.
I should like the minister to make a progress report, as it were, on this subject. I would be interested in knowing the circumstances under which those ponds are established, whether they are established on private property or on property that is held in the name of the provincial government, or under what circumstances they are provided. I must say that I approve most heartily of the idea but I am interested in knowing what the progress is, as are, I am sure, all the people in my province including a great many would-be anglers.
In addition, I should like the minister to make some comment on what progress is being made by the Atlantic salmon coordinating committee. A good many years ago-I suppose it is a couple of hundred years ago-the Atlantic salmon was a common fish. They abounded in the waters of eastern North America and in the St. Lawrence water system at one time as far up, I believe, as the Don river in what is now Toronto. They were, of course, common in Europe. I believe they were so common at one time that labourers, when taking employment, usually specified that they should not be fed Atlantic salmon more than five times a week or something of that sort. It had not been realized that it was such a great delicacy as it is considered at the present time, I suppose because familiarity breeds contempt. But with the development of obstructions in the streams and for other reasons, I presume, the Atlantic salmon population has gone down a great deal.
In my province of Prince Edward Island, Atlantic salmon are scarce. They do not occur at all in most streams. That, of course, was not the situation originally. When the first settlers came to that area I think most streams in Prince Edward Island abounded with Atlantic salmon. But early in our history small power dams were erected on the streams and they created obstructions for the fish, with the result that the fish which ordinarily came to spawn in those particular rivers were exterminated practically completely. Hence there have been no succeeding generations to come back.
I understand, however, that if young fish are put in a particular stream, a large percentage of them will return to spawn in that particular area, and that there should be no difficulty in restocking these streams if fish ladders could be constructed or some other means provided which would allow the fish to circumvent the obstructions which were built in the streams years ago and which still exist.
I should also like to mention a subject that is related to this problem. Perhaps the minister would be kind enough to state whether causeways which are now being built in connection with the trans-Canada highway, in the case of Prince Edward Island, are having any influence on the possible reproduction of fish in the area, or whether there are any oyster beds which would be affected by those causeways which, as I understand it, will maintain the tide upstream at a constant level. There would be other types of fish which might be affected, including smelts, of course, and trout.
There are some other things that I should like to mention but I shall not refer to them now. There are a few small items to which I should like to refer when the particular items come before the committee. However, I should like to make a reference to what has already been said by the hon. member for Gloucester with regard to poaching, especially in the lobster industry. I agree with him most heartily that if there could be put into operation an educational program which would educate the fishermen of the area as to the necessity for good conservation practices, the problem of poaching would decrease to a great extent. I most strongly recommend to the minister's consideration a careful study of the possibility of instituting a really effective educational program in that regard.

Supply-Fisheries
the explanations given by Dr. Pritchard, will be of tremendous value to the fishermen. I only hope these films can be brought to the fishermen along the coast. In this way perhaps the fishermen can be convinced that lobsters are not migratory, as Dr. Wilder and Dr. Pritchard maintain. These fishermen are quite intelligent, and they will see the advantage to their own industry of putting these small lobsters back into the water. Dr. Wilder said the increase in weight is 50 per cent in one year, so it is quite obvious to anyone who sees a film like that, with the splendid description Dr. Pritchard gave, that it is certainly in their own interests to put the small lobsters back into the water.
We have federal boats patrolling our coast. Many of the fishermen think the small lobsters should be brought to shore and released in shallow water. They claim that when the codfish are schooling the Northumberland strait on the north side of our province, the codfish gobble up the small lobsters. I have seen small lobsters in the maw of codfish.
In addition, I should like to suggest to the minister that we should have sufficient guardians or wardens to supervise the grading of the lobsters when the fishermen land them at the fishing centres. There are many centres in Prince Edward Island where there are always from three to six buyers, and if we had one warden located there as the fishermen were bringing in their fish they would be graded in a similar manner to potatoes when a farmer brings in a load. Potatoes are graded according to whether they are table potatoes or seed potatoes. Under the act the farmer has the protection of having these potatoes inspected at shipping points, and also under the seed certification branch. We are not prosecuted if our pack is not up to uniform standards across Canada. The cost would be very negligible.
For example, our guardians are willing to carry on that service for two months of the year and supply their own motor cars. The department pays them $145 per month, plus 9 cents per mile, I believe, for the use of their automobile, truck or whatever kind of motor vehicle they use. I note that according to the estimates of last year the department has reduced its expenditures by $344,000. In my opinion an industry as important as the fishing industry should have the estimates increased by that amount. I think we would be well repaid. I say the value of the fishing industry in Canada certainly entitles it to an increase in expenditure.
I do not believe we should have packers or fishermen prosecuted, haled into court and fined by magistrates or judges. In many cases,
[Mr. Kiekham.l
if the officer is arrogant he can prosecute any bona fide fisherman or packer. The packer employs a buyer, and he gives the buyer instructions not to take any small lobsters because if the inspectors come along when those small lobsters are on the sorting table they will not only prosecute the packer but if there are a thousand pounds of boiled lobsters on the table, large and small, they all go into bags and are taken by the prosecution officers to be distributed for charitable purposes. The packer, therefore, is subject to heavy losses. All this could be easily eliminated by giving us a few more land protection guardians and wardens. I think the value of the industry warrants it.
I should like now to say a word about the shell clam industry, which I believe could be developed to some extent. I refer to the quahaug. There is a splendid demand in the United States for what are called little neck quahaugs. There is also a good market in Canada for the hard shell or overgrown quahaugs that are available in the United States. The truck that delivers the little neck quahaugs to the United States could return with a load of the hard shell quahaugs. These are processed in Canada; they are ground up, and are one of the ingredients in Campbell's soup. This industry has been almost destroyed because of tariff restrictions by the United States.
Many of our leading packers and fishermen believe the quahaug industry could be developed tremendously by planting quahaug spat. What these people want is to be granted leases on the beaches that are favourable to the development of quahaugs. They are not asking for the privilege of exploiting the fishermen in the area who would normally drag the quahaugs when they reach a stage of development at which they can be marketed. These people are willing at their own expense, provided they obtain a lease from the department, to plant the quahaug spat and have them protected until such time as they can be properly harvested. I would like to ask the minister to look into the matter, and give it his earnest and favourable consideration.
I often recall, too, that some years ago the seagull was protected; and I think there was a very good reason for the protection of that bird because it decontaminated our shores of fish offal. The seagulls devoured the offal, thus eliminating the smells and making the area more attractive to tourists. Now, however, the situation has changed, because today no fish offal is made available to those birds; the offal is not thrown away. It is now taken to by-products plants and converted into fish meal.

I suggest to the minister that the time has come when we may have to destroy those predatory birds. Dr. Pritchard mentioned the other evening that a nine-inch lobster deposits 75,000 lobster berries, and those berries float on the surface for one month after they are discharged from the female lobster. It might be that the seagulls, which are not divers and do not bring up deteriorated fish from the bottom, could pick up large quantities of the lobster berries. I would ask the minister to look into this phase of the matter.
But in addition to predatory birds we have predatory humans, and they have come from the province of New Brunswick. Those predatory humans exhaust our shores of clams. Just in that connection I would like to read what our protection officer had to say on the subject:
There is an increase in the bar clam landings of some 107 hundredweight, a decrease in clams of 799 hundredweight and a decrease in quahaugs of over 4000 hundredweight. Most of our soft shell clam beds are depleted and it is difficult at the present time to find enough for shore picnics on beds that used to produce barrels daily. The landed value of these varieties was down by some $13,000.
So they have taken our clams. That is quite legal, of course; I am not complaining about it. However, clams are pretty poor bait.
I do not think I shall take any more time. I only wish to emphasize before taking my seat that I would like to see some more modern method of dealing with bona fide fishermen and packers, rather than the present system of prosecution. Some of these fishermen are subject to large fines. I do not know who benefits from those fines the fishermen pay. It may be the dominion government, or perhaps the province; I am not sure. However, I would re-emphasize that I am sure the minister and his deputy have the interest of the fishermen at heart, and will rectify this method of prosecution.

Mr. Chairman, during the course of this debate the majority of the speakers have hailed from the Atlantic coast. Lest there be any chance that this chamber should overlook the fact that we have an important fishing industry on the Pacific coast, I think it behooves me to make a few comments regarding the speech delivered by the minister this morning.
I do not want the committee to be under any false impression that the importance of the fishing industry on the Atlantic seaboard as compared with that on the Pacific has any relation whatsoever to the number of members who are speaking, because it must be kept in mind that the number of members speaking on this subject is governed by the
Supply-Fisheries
number of constituencies on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. It so happens there are about five Atlantic seaboard constituencies for each one on the Pacific coast.
I would call attention to the fact that the hon. member for Queens missed entirely the point in the story he told, of how years ago certain workmen had it written into their contracts that they were not to be fed Atlantic salmon more than five days a week. Of course they wanted that provision; it was British Columbia salmon they were insisting upon. And I would like my friend from Saint John-Albert also to forgo his continual praise-and in this he has been joined by others-of the anaemic salmon which come from the Atlantic seaboard. It is the red-blooded salmon we really want.
Can they vote?
No, the salmon cannot vote, but the salmon on the Pacific coast are certainly Canadian babies.
And you migh; get some suckers, too.

I was very pleased to hear about the very satisfactory conditions in the fishing industry on the Pacific coast, as reported by the minister in his opening speech. I think I heard him correctly when he said there is no surplus. By this I understand there is no carryover of stock from a year ago. According to reports from the industry, on April 30 of this year there was a carryover of more than 350,000 cases. If that has been sold-and from what the minister has said, I would assume it has-that is very creditable indeed, because the industry on the west coast is highly competitive. We have to compete with the beef and other meats raised on the prairies, and we also have to compete with other nations in the fishing industry.
We have to watch very carefully the increase in the Japanese fishing fleet, and the excellent product being turned out by Japan and sold in Canada. I have no quarrel with that, because Japan has to sell its products, but we have to be able to compete with the Japanese. I am not quite certain that we should not carry out investigations to see if the style of can and the way in which our product is put up might not be improved. I know that today the skin and bones are included in the can. I suppose there are trade reasons for that, but when you empty a can of salmon I sometimes think it is not quite as appetizing as it might be.
There was another point I was pleased to note; that is, that the long negotiations between the fishermen and the canning companies had been concluded in time so the fleet could leave for the northern waters on

Supply-Fisheries
the day the sockeye salmon fishing season opened. In years gone by negotiations have been carried on for long periods of time and the fleet has not been able to get away in order to take advantage of the full season.
I want to refer to the agreement which I hope will be successfully concluded this year with reference to pink salmon, somewhat along the lines of the sockeye salmon commission. I spoke on this matter last year, and it is most important to our fishermen on the west coast. It is not only a case of an agreement being reached; additional facilities should be provided for our fishermen in order that they may catch their full quota of pinks as compared with the United States fishermen, who have the advantage of large ships and safe harbours along the southern shore of San Juan strait. We are short of harbours other than Victoria. Sooke harbour needs dredging badly; and while there is an excellent harbour at the entrance of the San Juan river, it is open to gales from the southeast which sweep right across, with rollers coming in from cape Flattery. I do not know whether it would be practical to construct some sort of shelter or cove or breakwater of some kind to protect the fishermen's vessels, but I would hope that something could be done. My information is only from local sources, but I believe the minister has had his officials look into this.
The next point I wanted to refer to was the question of the limitation of licences. I spoke about this last year, when I urged that licences be restricted to Canadian citizens and also that there should be a line of demarcation drawn between the legitimate commercial fishermen and the part-time fishermen. A professional or businessman may take holidays of two weeks to a month while the salmon run is on, and he will go out with a commercial licence for only a short period. Actually he is infringing on the legitimate fishermen. Common sense must be used in dealing with this matter, as we want to encourage sport fishing, but a limitation on licences is required.
There was one remark the minister made which caused me great concern. He referred to the investigations being carried on in connection with utilizing the meat of the dogfish. He said this might be turned into fish meal, which is an excellent idea because it could then be used on the numerous mink farms on the coast. But he went on to say that it might also be used in fish and chip shops, and then went a step further and referred to the fish and chip shops in the same breath as hot dog stands. That certainly made my hackles rise. I want to assure
[Mr. Pearkes.l
the minister that we have some excellent fish and chip shops in my constituency. If he will let me know the next time he visits Victoria I will take him down where he can have an excellent meal.
May I correct that now. The fish and chip shops I was referring to are in England, where there is a large consumption through those outlets. Dogfish are not used in fish and chip shops in Canada.

I was afraid the minister was going to suggest that they might be. If you are going to introduce dogfish into the excellent fish and chip shops on Vancouver island you will have to do a very high class job of salesmanship.
The English do.

You had better put your research experts to trying to find a trade name for it in order to help you out. Perhaps I can help your officials in that respect. During the dinner recess I went to the library to see if I could get any help, and I found that the dogfish comes from many different families of fish. The most prevalent one in the Pacific is the squali dae or the carcharii dae. It seems to me that that suggests a trade name. Instead of calling them dogfish and chips possibly you might refer to them as a succulent squalus sandwich or something like that. There would have to be a good job of selling them done. I assure the minister that we have a number of excellent fish and chip shops there which serve the best halibut they can get.
If when closing the debate on this item the minister can give me some assurance about the commission and about the licences, we will let the hot dogfish and chips business stand for the time being.

Mr. Chairman, what I have to say will be brief because this is one department about which I do not know very much. My problem is not markets or canning or fishing, it is what is happening to our fish. I was glad the minister said something this afternoon about fish being killed through the pollution of our rivers. While I did not hear what he had to say, I am glad to know that he is interested in this problem and I hope something will be done about it.
When the question of the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river came up last year the minister told us he had no jurisdiction over fish in interprovincial rivers. I am hoping he will become interested enough to try to make some arrangements with the provinces so that fish in interprovincial rivers may be looked after by the federal Department of Fisheries instead of by the different

provincial departments. At present it is not possible to safeguard fish in an interprovincial river where pollution takes place in one province and the fish are killed in another. I plead with the minister to do something about these fish. We have not very many fish in my constituency except those in the lakes, but quite frequently people do go down to our rivers to fish.
There is another problem in connection with the pollution of rivers which is closely connected to but much more important than our fish population. I hope the minister will consider this matter seriously. We have had before us legislation under which the dominion government is going to take jurisdiction over international rivers. They should take a good look at this problem of the pollution of interprovincial rivers and try to arrive at some agreement with the provinces or bring forward some kind of legislation at the next session which will protect our fish population as well as our human population.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps one of the greatest tributes one could pay to the Minister of Fisheries' speech today is that someone like myself from a residential area in the middle of an island which has no fisheries whatsoever found it both interesting and informative. I do not know whether in the few minutes I have been away from this debate someone may have said this, but I want to express my personal hope that the minister has a pleasant trip to Russia and, most important, that he gets back here safely. I think there are some of us who would miss him a great deal more than we would miss others we might send.
I was not too impressed with the discussion on the relative merits of British Columbia salmon versus maritime salmon, because in Quebec we know we have the biggest and best fish in the world. At a convention in Quebec about three years ago they presented a British Columbia salmon and a maritime salmon to the chairman. We did not know what happened to ours, but we finally checked and found they could not even get the Quebec salmon through the door of the hotel.
Throughout this debate there has been running a thread of worry about the consumption of fish products in Canada, and a desire that the consumption of those fish products be increased. That is what brings me to my feet tonight. While some of us from cities may know little about fisheries, along the way we may have learned a little about merchandising products. One in that position cannot help but be impressed and disappointed on examining the expenditure-or perhaps I should
Supply-Fisheries
say the lack of expenditure-by the fisheries department in the promotion of fish as a food. I am thinking primarily in this case of advertising, exhibitions and publicity.
Let me say at once that I know the department has done what they consider and many people consider to be a good job, and certainly it is a job far in advance of that which was being done a few years ago. But when we turn to the actual items we find that their total expenditure in advertising and other means of promoting the sale of fish is to be some $93,000.
When we compare that with some of the other expenditures for the same type of operation, that is for advertising, publicity and so on, we find, for example, the post office with $192,000; we find the labour department with $245,000; we find the Department of Citizenship and Immigration with $103,000; and there are a number of others which I shall not go into. In a number of cases these expenditures on behalf of advertising, publicity and so forth can very justifiably be criticized. Certainly they should be examined with great care in the light of the use which we sometimes find is being made of the money.
