In the case of the fisheries of Canada, where we have an industry worth over $200 million and where we have to provide for increased consumption and increased utilization of their output, it would seem to me that to find the fisheries department one of the lowest spenders in this field is curious when we couple it with their expressed desire to increase the utilization of fish.
For example, here we have an interesting comparison. The Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, which is primarily responsible for encouraging tourism in Canada, spends just over a million dollars, $1,080,000, in this field of advertising. For that expenditure they bring to Canada some $275 million worth of tourist spending. That is the 1951 figure. Yet we have a fisheries industry with almost the same volume of business, with some 83,000 people employed in one way or another, and we find them spending a comparatively small amount in this field.
Again we can make the comparison with private industry. In private industry they consider an expenditure of perhaps 5 per cent of the gross value of their products for advertising purposes not at all out of line. If you include the other sales efforts, it would be substantially in excess of that. This would indicate a budget to encourage the sale of fish products in Canada of some $10 million a year.

Supply-Fisheries
Let me make it plain at once that I am not advocating or suggesting that this should be spent entirely, or even largely, by the government. I do feel, however, that they should give leadership in this respect, and that brings me to the particular suggestion which I would put forth, having first of all presented the idea to the minister. That is that he explore with the fisheries industry, perhaps through the fisheries council or perhaps with some of the firms therein, the possibility of the government, on a matching basis with industry, subsidizing an expanded campaign to encourage the consumption of fish in Canada.
I do not think for a moment that the fishing industry, any more than any other industry, is entitled to have government money spent on its behalf without putting up some of its own money, but I do think that the government might well take the leadership in this field and perhaps thereby increase the consumption of fish sizeably.
In that connection, I do not know whether or not this story is apocryphal, but it is said that some years ago one of the canners in British Columbia was left with a great stock of salmon on his hands which had been packed in white condition for some reason.
That is a fable.

As
we all know, salmon is usually pink. He had a great deal of difficulty in selling the salmon. Finally he got a good advertising man who advised him to advertise it as salmon guaranteed not to turn pink in the can. Within a matter of months he had cleaned the stock of salmon out of his warehouse, to his very great delight. I think we would all be happy if that type of forward thinking could come from the fisheries department to supplement the very good job they have already done in starting the campaign of public information on the use and consumption of fish in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister on the very interesting and comprehensive survey of the activities of his department which he gave us this morning, and also on the thorough knowledge which he displayed of all the different kinds of work his department carries on. I should like to thank him also for his announcement with regard to the rebate on salt. This is a form of assistance to the salt fish industry which I believe will be appreciated by all fishermen.
Deficiency payments may have served a useful purpose, but we must not lose sight of the fact that they have some disadvantages in

that they tend to reduce the incentive for intensive bargaining on the part of the exporters. The end result could very well be that the real beneficiary of the deficiency payments is not the fisherman himself but the foreign purchaser of our product.
I am particularly pleased that this assistance to the salt fish industry has taken this form, because I think it is a recognition that one of the major problems in connection with our salt fish industry is the purchase and distribution of salt. I am glad to know that during the year a careful study is to be made in order to determine whether present methods of purchasing, packaging and distribution of salt can be improved in order to further reduce the cost to the fishermen.
In this respect I should like to suggest that some recommendation be made whereby salt would be sold by weight in all provinces instead of by volume, as it is now sold in my own province. In Newfoundland we buy and sell salt by the hogshead, which is a unit of volume. It is a well known fact that when these barrels are filled up by people shovelling salt into them, there is a wide variation in the amount of salt that is required to fill the barrels, depending on the skill of the person shovelling it in.
There is a real need for more standardization in the salting of our fish. There is still too much left to chance; there is still too great a variation between the amounts of salt used by different individuals in salting the same amount of fish. This is true both with regard to the light salted cure and the heavy salted cure. It would seem to me that if a unit of weight were substituted for a unit of volume, it would be a simple matter to remedy this situation, because once the salinity of the salt is known it should not be difficult to carry out experiments in order to determine just what weight of salt is necessary to salt a certain amount of fish for a certain period of time, whether it be for the light salted cure or for the heavy salted cure.
In this respect I also think some experiments should be carried out in order to determine the proper heights of fish piles, because when the piles of salted fish exceed a certain height, the weight of the fish on top presses the salt out from the fish on the bottom, and we do not then have a uniform amount of pickle throughout the whole bulk. This is particularly true when the fish is salted at sea and piled up in a ship's hold. When this fish is unloaded a great deal of allowance must be made, more by guess than anything else, to average out the amount of pickle or the amount of salt in the fish being weighed.

I was greatly interested in the experiment with the motorized dories to which the minister referred this morning. I hope the experiment will not be abandoned or written off as a failure, because I do not think it really had a fair trial. I have discussed this matter with experienced bank skippers, and find they are of the opinion that the experiment could be successful. I think the results already obtained have proved that for the fishing days, a greater amount of fish was caught per man in this way than was caught by the ordinary method. It was unfortunate that this experiment was undertaken in the fall of the year and at a time when the weather turned extremely stormy, so that few fishing days were possible while the experiment was in progress.
We are all interested in what the minister said this morning about the conferences that are being carried out with respect to our territorial waters. We must at some time know just to where our territorial waters extend. We certainly cannot put in any sort of patrol service unless we establish definite territorial limits. I think everyone will agree that while the achieving of international agreement may be a more difficult and slower process, yet perhaps in the end it will turn out to be the most satisfactory method. At the same time I think we must not lose sight of the fact that the time may come when it will be necessary to think not in terms of territorial waters but in terms of extending our sovereignty over the sea floor. Present defence developments may make that procedure necessary, and I think we should keep it constantly in mind.
We are all happy to know that some measures are going to be studied to conserve our herd of Atlantic seals. That herd has diminished to a mere fraction of its former size, and unless something is done there is danger that it will become altogether extinct. In this connection may I say that a number of our sealers this year shipped on Norwegian vessels operating out of Halifax, and it was surprising to many of us to note the great difference in the earnings of those people who shipped on Norwegian boats as compared with the earnings of those who shipped on local boats. I wonder whether the minister, when he replies, could give us any information as to the reason for the great disparity in the earnings of the two sets of individuals, when the catch of seals was approximately the same.
I should like to support what my friend the hon. member for Kings said with respect to the operation of draggers on inshore fishing grounds. Whatever may be the effect of intensive dragging operations on the larger
Supply-Fisheries
fishing grounds, I think it has been established that the small inshore fishing grounds could well be destroyed and made useless unless dragging operations are restricted.
I should like to congratulate the minister and his department on the emphasis which his inspection service is now placing on education rather than police action. I think this is a move in the right direction and one that will bear very great results.
I hope the minister and his officials will keep in mind the need for a flexible bait service in my province. I know it is the only province in which the federal government operates a bait service, but it was one of the commitments under the terms of union, and a very necessary one born out of our experience over a great many years.
With respect to bait, I would urge the minister to place greater emphasis on the securing of squid, because squid bait is a universal bait. It can be used all the year round. It is a bait that will stand up well under processes of refrigeration and thawing, and is superior to all other forms of bait we use.

Mr. Chairman, coming as I do from the Pacific coast I would have hardly dared enter this debate if it had not been that my honourable and gallant friend from Esquimalt-Saanich had led the militant forces of the Pacific coast in voicing our importance. On the other hand, of course, the fact that in my constituency there is perhaps the most important installation of the fisheries department in Canada would lead me to enter it. As a British Columbian I would point out that it was not until the Prime Minister of Canada reached into the province of British Columbia to get a minister that we had anything in the nature of vigour or efficiency in the administration of this department.
I remember that many years ago when I was in the provincial house and the present Minister of Fisheries was a bright young man assisting a provincial cabinet minister, we used to have almost annually a day on which the members of all parties, including cabinet ministers, spent a happy hour hurling recriminations at distant Ottawa because of the fact that the Department of Fisheries did nothing on the coast of British Columbia. In fact I remember there was a serious move on foot to appeal to Ottawa either to undertake the responsibility or to pass it over to the provincial government. I am happy to agree with other members today in the view it is a very good thing that did not happen, because we have had great advances in the fisheries department.

Supply-Fisheries
There are one or two points I should like to draw to the minister's attention. He spoke in his address of his attempt, shall I say, to encourage diplomatic fishing in order to persuade our American neighbours to make an agreement with us with regard to the fishing of the pinks in the strait of Juan de Fuca. I should like to remind the minister that, while I am all in favour of doing that, quite possibly our American friends may embarrass us by reminding us of the continued existence in the strait of Juan de Fuca of the fish traps at Sooke which, as we all know, have been a sort of subdued thorn in the flesh of international harmony for a long time. I suggest to the minister that he examine our position in that regard when he is trying to get some sort of agreement with the Americans on the fishing in the strait of Juan de Fuca.
There is another matter which, while it does not really fall within the Department of Fisheries, concerns the department and the minister very acutely. That is the question of a coastguard service on the Pacific coast. I know quite well that the minister has had representations from every fishermen's organization on the Pacific coast pointing out that the present arrangements are totally inadequate to safeguard life and property. I should like to see the minister urge his colleague the Minister of Transport to reconsider the question of the establishment of a coastguard service on our Pacific coast.
Then there is another matter that directly concerns the Department of Public Works but is also of great importance to the fishermen. That is the question of harbours on the east coast of Vancouver island. Over the last 12 months I have been making representations to the Department of Public Works with regard to the extension of the breakwater at Northwest bay. I have not been successful. I did succeed in persuading the department to extend or replace the log floats they now have anchored at the end of the rock fill, but I would suggest this is a totally inadequate and rather uneconomical way of providing the kind of shelter the fishermen on that particular part of the coast require in rough weather. Again, I should like to see the minister make representations to his colleague the Minister of Public Works to reconsider the question of safe harbourage for fishermen on the east coast of Vancouver island.
We have heard a great deal about lobsters in the Atlantic. I do not suppose the minister will tell us anything about the attempt with respect to lobsters on the Pacific coast. I know it is a matter of great secrecy that they

have been planted there; there is a veil of secrecy like that over the defence estimates. We think they are still there, but we do not know. Rumours fly around. I wonder whether the minister, without giving away any secrets, can tell us just how successful the transplanting project has been, or whether his officials know how successful it has been. Finally-and it is not really British Columbian patriotism that makes me draw this matter to the attention of hon. members who are not unfortunate enough to live on the other side of the Rocky mountains-
That is a good phrase.

-I would remind them of the installation I mentioned when I started, the marine biological station at Nanaimo, which is not only the most important installation of the department on the Pacific coast but one of the world's leading marine biological stations, a station of very great importance and prestige of which all Canadians should be extremely proud.
I should also like to join with the minister and other members in paying tribute to the excellent services of the officials of the Department of Fisheries. My only criticism of the minister is that I should like to see him present even more vigorously than I am sure he has done the claims of these gentlemen to much more adequate salaries than they receive at the present time. Like the minister, I am quite dubious about the relative values of lawyers and scientists. I have a very irreverent suspicion that scientists are perhaps a little more valuable to our society than lawyers, and if we are going to treat the lawyers very well we had better treat the scientists even more generously or there will be nothing with which to provide lawyers' fees.

Mr. Chairman, while I do not represent any commercial fishermen I do represent the mecca of sport fishing in the interior of British Columbia. I assure the minister I shall not be long, but I should like to take a minute or two to say a few words.
I must say first of all that I enjoyed his excellent review of the department's activities. It was most informative and interesting. The minister can be quite provocative on occasion, but I always notice that when he presents his estimates he does so in such good style that -he completely disarms the opposition and they go through with very little criticism.
However, I rose particularly to draw his attention to one very serious omission in his presentation to the house. If I heard him correctly, he dealt with the fishing derbies on the coast and rather proudly informed the

house of the fact that these extensive fishing derbies were being carried on. We are very pleased to hear that, but coming from British Columbia as he does I am sure he would wish to see the record completed before his estimates are passed. I hope that in his future representations to the house he will recognize the fact that there is a large fishing derby on the upper Arrow lakes, another on the lower Arrow lakes, and another on Kootenay lake, all conducted by the various rod and gun associations.
I just rise, Mr. Chairman, because, whether or not you are aware of it, we have an excellent sport fishing district which attracts a very large number of tourists every year, and possibly this slight addition to the record will help that business.

Just let me say
a word about advertising. I only rise because of what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert had to say. He blamed members of parliament for not advertising fish sufficiently. I believe the low consumption of fish is directly related to advertising. The department publishes very good booklets containing recipes, but I do not think the distribution of these booklets is adequate. A person has to write in for them. I managed to get a few, and I distributed them. In fact I gave some of them to one of the retail fish men in Peterborough, and he distributed those booklets to the people. They asked for more.
I have one suggestion to make, and that is my reason for rising. I believe there would be a better chance of encouraging people to use fish if you just had a single sheet containing a recipe on each side which could be given to the retail fish merchant to wrap up with the fish. Perhaps 100 of these a month could be given to each retail fish dealer. In these booklets there are a lot of highbrow recipes, and there are some plain ones. What you have to do is sell the fish to the person with a small income, and the person with a small income is buying frozen fish. Many of those people do not know how to cook it properly. There may be some directions printed on the label, but people should be told of more than one way in which to cook that fish.
I believe the minister or his department should publish some better directions for cooking these frozen fillets. The dealer could wrap the fish in these single sheets containing the recipes, and I believe you would sell more fish. I know that is so, because I have heard housewives speak about it.

I must first thank all hon. members, Mr. Chairman, for the very generous praise they have directed, not so much
Supply-Fisheries
at me as at the work of the Department of Fisheries, the officers and staff. The member for Kootenay West said there were times when I was provocative. If he will recall, those were the times when I was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, and when the measures I was putting forward did not get the same praise from every quarter of the house. In those days I used to feel that the best defence was a quick offence.
I am going to go through the points in order, as raised by hon. members. I think when we finish those we may carry the rest of the estimates fairly quickly, because they seem to have covered most of the later items.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and many others were full of praise for the excellent work which had been done by our consumers' branch in extending the sale of fish. Our staff dietitians who visit schools, restaurant associations and women's clubs to teach fish cookery and prepare cook books, have done a good job. There was criticism from one member because the expenditure in connection with this item was lower this year. This is because last year we bought four station wagons for our dietitians in the larger cities of Canada, to enable them to visit the outlying schools. This is a nonrecurring expenditure.
It is quite true that the first aim of our department should be to increase the consumption of fish in our home market. We are doing that in every way we can. Since I have been minister I certainly have spoken on many platforms, over the radio and even appeared on T.V. trying to urge the consumption of more fish.
So far as the tariff on fish sticks is concerned, that is primarily a matter for the Department of Trade and Commerce. It was a matter of regret to us to see that increase in the tariff on cooked fish sticks. We have this close relationship with the United States industry. As the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond pointed out, more and more the United States market is going to have to depend on our fishermen for their supplies. We hope there will be an adjustment in that tariff in the not too distant future.
Every year the problem of the conflict between our own inshore fishermen, that is the fishermen in small boats who come back home every night, and our bigger boats is raised. The inshore fisherman, of course, wants the big boats kept out. Our department is trying to modernize the fleet and encourage the building of these bigger boats, draggers, long-liners and trawlers, for more effective fishing. It is rather difficult when we do that to then tell the men they have

Supply-Fisheries
to go far away from shore. There is certainly no positive answer to the problem, but we try to work out a satisfactory compromise between the inshore fishermen and the deep sea fishermen. We did put the draggers out of St. Margaret's bay, and in St. Mary's bay, mentioned by the hon. member, we confined dragging to draggers of less than 40 feet. After all, those are rather small boats.
The report of the interdepartmental committee on territorial waters is at present before the Department of External Affairs. The minister said it would be made public after it had been studied by the government. I shall certainly draw the attention of the Minister of Transport, as I already have, to the new requirements of steamship inspection of fishing boats and the qualifications for skippers and mates. It is quite true these boats do not carry passengers and should not be subject to the same rigorous standards as ships that do carry passengers. Of course, they can collide with passenger ships, so there is reason for some standards. The standards certainly should not be as severe as those imposed on people who are skippers or mates of passenger ships.
The hon. member for Comox-Albemi spoke of the damage done to spawning grounds by logging operations. That is true not only in British Columbia but right in the Atlantic provinces too. At one time there was a substantial salmon fishery in Ontario, but as the forests were logged and turned into farm lands the water was no longer held in the ground but ran off quickly and the gravel beds silted up so the salmon found it impossible to spawn. We do watch that very closely on the west coast. Last year our engineering staff cleared 135 salmon streams. We have a total of 1.600 salmon streams on the west coast, so it is quite a job, but we do watch that. We get co-operation from the logging companies and from all industry in British Columbia.
The hon. member spoke of the fact that in one part of his riding there is not the happy relation between the sports fishermen and the commercial fishermen that exists in other parts of the province. There is a conflict between the sports and commercial fishermen who operate along the east coast of Vancouver island because of the presence of the big salmon and herring seiners in that area. This summer we are going to work out a program for keeping the big ships farther off shore and allowing the sports fishermen to have the immediate offshore fisheries.
He spoke, too, about the disparity between the incomes of Newfoundland fishermen and

British Columbia fishermen. This is true, but the British Columbia fishermen are highly organized. They are catching a fish which is very desirable in the market, and so they do get better returns. My aim, as Minister of Fisheries, is to try to lift the income of the Newfoundland fishermen up to the level of the British Columbia fishermen. By that time the British Columbia fishermen will be far ahead again.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for New Westminster spoke again about the closure on the upper Fraser which I announced last year to the fishermen's union. It was enforced last year and is being enforced again this year. This is not an overnight decision at all, but has been discussed for 50 years. About 50 years ago a royal commission recommended it. It is the result of two things, the ever-increasing pressure on our salmon fisheries, and the fact that these upper river fishermen in this area are in a very privileged group. Most of them do not fish more than one day a week, the reason being that the only day worth fishing is the first day after the week-end closure. On opening day the downstream fishermen get the bulk of the fish, so few are available upstream after the first day.
To hear the hon. member speak you would think these men were out of the fishing business completely. Of course that is not so. I had a full report of the fishing effort up there made during the past year. They still have the full spring salmon fishing from February 1 to June 30. They have the main sockeye salmon fishing from July 1 to September 15. The river is generally closed on this date, anyway. The last season is the fall fishing for pinks and chums. These spawn in streams quite close to the entrance to the river, and are fish which decline in quality very quickly once they enter fresh water. They are best caught in the sea, where quality is high.
It is these fish which can no longer be caught in the up-river area. These fishermen still have the right to fish down the river in this period, or to do as the great bulk of the fishermen do-fish out at sea. The up-river fishermen still have at least three-quarters of their fishery left, and they can certainly adjust themselves to being full-time fishermen, as are the fishermen of my riding and of the riding of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, and the hon. member for Skeena, and the member for any other coastal riding.

And could they not use the
same gear?

That is why I think today they are privileged fishermen. They fish part

of a river not much wider in places than this chamber, with small boats and nets, and expect to be given special privileges as against those other fishermen who fish the high seas in good weather and in bad.
The hon. member for Charlotte was worried about the decrease in the herring and sardine fisheries over last year in the bay of Fundy. These fish do come in great cycles, along with fluctuation during the course of a season. We are doing the thing he suggested, a joint investigation, now under way with the fisheries department in the state of Maine, because in the United States the fisheries are under state control.
Then the hon. members for Saint John-Albert and Queens asked about the catch of Atlantic salmon. So far as commercial fishermen are concerned, it has gone up steadily. In 1952 it was two million pounds; in 1953,
2,713,000	pounds and in 1954 it was 3,676,000 pounds. The angling catch has gone down, from 490,000 pounds in 1952 to 402,000 pounds in 1953; and for last year the present estimate is something less than 400,000 pounds.
There are reasons for this; increased industrialization of New Brunswick, a greatly increased number of sports fishermen down in those streams, the effect of power dams, the effect of logging so far as the run-off of the streams is concerned, and the effect of the spraying for the spruce budworm, all have had their toll on salmon which spend their first three years in these streams.
He said the poor Saint John fishermen had no powerful lobby up here to speak for them. Well, last fall I met an association of all the great fishing clubs, composed mostly of men who are very wealthy, and who lease fishing rights on the New Brunswick rivers. They complained very bitterly about the powerful lobby of these net fishermen, who had more votes than they did, and they felt I was catering to the net fishermen rather than to the sports fishermen in the fishing clubs.
However, that is not so. We want a salmon industry which will support both a large commercial operation and a large angling operation, just as we have it on the west coast; and our program of conservation now enforced will, we hope, bring this about.
He also spoke about the problem of the gaspereau. In a year when the catch of a fishery is down there always comes a request for the extension of the season so the fishermen can increase their catch. But that is the very year when we cannot afford to extend the season, because we must cut down on the fishing effort to make sure there are sufficient spawners left to build up the catch in succeeding years.
Supply-Fisheries
He commented on the relative values of the Atlantic and Pacific salmon. Well, as Minister of Fisheries of course I should be neutral. But I will say just this one thing; it is just a matter of where you eat the fish. Fish is best when it is fresh, and certainly spring salmon out on the west coast is at least the equal of any salmon down on the east coast. Here in Ottawa, Atlantic salmon generally comes fresh whereas Pacific salmon is frozen; and frozen fish or meat or fruit does not have the texture or the flavour of the fresh article. I will say, however, that after my experience last year fishing Atlantic salmon, Atlantic salmon is a better sporting fish than our west coast fish.
The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond paid a deserved tribute to the great work done by fishermen's co-operatives in the maritime provinces in helping the fishing industry.
The hon. member for Selkirk asked why we do not extend all the benefits of federal fisheries legislation to the fishermen of the prairie provinces. Well, the reason is that we have not control of those fisheries. Any fisheries legislation which needs the administration of our officers cannot be given in those areas, because we have no staff there. Because of this, many of the fishermen in these areas feel that perhaps all commercial fisheries, instead of just the coastal commercial fisheries, should be handled by the federal department. If that were so, then we could have all federal legislation apply to all commercial fisheries in Canada.
The hon. member for Gloucester spoke about the good work we are doing in lobster conservation, especially in the matter of the education of fishermen to realize that conservation is, in the long run, in their interests. He spoke about the necessity of having bilingual officers in his riding, and with that I agree. So far as scientists go, I would say to him that good fisheries scientists are so rare that we are satisfied if we get one who speaks one of the two official languages, just so long as he is a good scientist. Then we do, of course, translate all our regulations and instructions.
The hon. member for New Westminster spoke about the Fraser river closure, and asked about the variation in the pink salmon catch in the Fraser river. It is a very odd fishery, because in one year we have almost no fish at all and in the next year we have as many as ten million fish. This variation is one of the things which the scientists are studying. The large Canadian catch in 1939-41 was due mainly, I believe, to the fishing strike on the United States side. It is

Supply-Fisheries
only in the last year that we have been able in a normal season to build our catch up to 40 per cent.
He asked how we are enforcing area boundaries between gill netters and seiners out on the gulf. Well, we do it by our protective service, by taking them to police court and fining them and, if necessary, confiscating the fish they have caught and cancelling licences. We have had no complaints from the unions about our enforcement of the fisheries boundaries.
The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador asked how the fishermen in his area find out whether our exploratory fishing is successful. My reply would be that they find out in the easiest way known. If they see our exploratory boats come in with lots of fish, they ask immediately and follow them back to sea. Long before the results are published the fishermen pretty well know where the new banks are. He suggested the quality of salt cod would be improved if we paid a premium on quality production. That is one thing we will study this year. Premiums are paid to encourage the production of better bacon, better cheese, and so on, and it may be that it would help raise the quality of cod production.
The hon. member for Queens asked first of all about sports fishing in the national parks. That is closely related to sports fishing in the province where the park is situated. The regulations are similar, and we work together on research. He spoke about the need for improved public works for fishermen. My colleague the Minister of Public Works is the member for Queens-Lunenburg, a great fishing district. His father was the skipper of a banker schooner for many years, so he is well informed as to the needs of fishermen. When our department does put forward a proposal for public works for the fishing industry, I have found him very sympathetic.
The fresh water fisheries of Prince Edward Island are under our control. We have done a lot of work in encouraging the stocking of speckled and rainbow trout. The streams of Prince Edward Island are the most accessible of any in the country. It is the garden island and you can drive along close to any stream, so the fishing pressure of anglers on these streams is heavy because the streams are so accessible.
The hon. member for Kings asked if it was possible to cure the poaching of lobsters by education. We think the most immediate way of curing it is by police action, and we are following that by education in the hope that in the end police action will not be necessary. The hon. member spoke also about

the grading of lobsters. We have not yet found that necessary because there is such keen demand among buyers of lobsters from the fishermen, which is the best assurance that the fisherman is going to get a good price.
The hon. member, and many others, including quite a number of Conservative members, deplored the decrease in my estimates. I am glad the Minister of Finance is here. I had four years with the Department of Finance and I have listened to a number of Conservative members urge reductions in the estimates. I thought I was going to be applauded when, after having combed through our department, we were able to reduce the estimates by $300,000, but I did not get any thanks for that saving. As a matter of fact I should not be ungrateful, because hon. members have suggested that we should spend more and the Minister of Finance is present tonight and has had a chance to hear them make that sound suggestion.
The hon. member for Kings also made a novel suggestion, that we should attempt the controlling of seagulls. We do control the mergansers which do such damage to salmon spawn in the maritimes, but seagulls are protected by law because they are such great scavengers. They are graceful birds and they serve a most useful purpose in keeping the sea clean.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich referred to our record sockeye pack. We have still some in storage, but it is sold. We will have a lighter pack of sockeye this year, but a bigger pack of pinks. It is quite true that our present machine-packed salmon is not as attractive as the old hand-packed was, but with the cost of labour on the west coast the fishing industry cannot afford to pack salmon by hand in cans and still have it compete in price with Russian and Japanese salmon.
The hon. member, along with many others, referred to the need of a pink salmon treaty and also the need for better harbours on the outer west coast of Vancouver island to serve this developing deep-sea fleet. The Department of Public Works is now studying how to build a breakwater at San Juan in that exposed area.
I can assure the hon. member that I did not suggest that fish and chip shops in Canada should use dogfish. It would help if they did, for fresh dogfish is said to be edible if it is well cooked. If the English can eat it in such quantities there is no reason why we could not as well.
The hon. member for The Battlefords spoke about the pollution of rivers on the prairies. The main problem is that the administration

of fisheries in the prairies is under the three provincial governments. If a river is interprovincial it is most difficult for one province to do anything about pollution which occurs in another province. We have helped wtih scientific advice on methods of handling the problem.
The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace spoke as a representative of the consumers in Canada. That is the most important group to the fishing industry, and we wish we had more consumers in Canada, not only more but bigger. The hon. member deplored the lack of advertising by our department. I hope my colleagues from the other departments will note that I have been criticized not for spending too much, but for spending too little in the way of advertising and public relations.
We have worked out an arrangement with the fishing industry which we regard as quite reasonable. We do the public relations work by way of education through our consumer branch with cook books, lectures, film strips, institutional advertising and so on, while the industry itself undertakes the advertising of brand names. The west coast industry has been especially active. It is a highly organized industry of big companies and can do this. On the east coast there are many smaller industries and therefore they do not have the same resources to institute large brand name campaigns. The other departments of government which he mentioned, such as the post office and citizenship and immigration, are not associated with industries and so must do all their own advertising.
did not praise them for spending money.

The hon. member did not praise me for not spending money. The hon. member repeated one of the oldest fables in the salmon industry, the fable of the white salmon. We actually have a race of white spring salmon on the west coast but they are very seldom packed in cans; they are sold fresh and smoked. It is nice to know that one of the oldest chestnuts in the fishing industry has got as far east as Montreal.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo spoke of means of improving the distribution of salt by packing it in bags rather than in these large hogsheads, and by standardizing the quality. He spoke of Newfoundland sealers being paid better wages when they work on Norwegian ships than when they work on Newfoundland ships. The reason for that is that the men on Norwegian ships get a share of the skins and the oil of the catch, while the men on Newfoundland ships share only in the oil. Perhaps if the Newfoundland men organized they might be able

I am suggesting that the matter of organization is one for the fishermen themselves.
The hon. member for Nanaimo referred to the fish traps at Sooke. I think they are on the way out. Five licences are held, but they have not all been used for some years. The most to be put down lately have been three, because the fishing companies now find it cheaper to use seiners than to drive piles each year. The fish traps are a dying industry.
The hon. member referred to the need of a coastguard service, which is a matter of great concern to the fishing industry. The R.C.A.F. sea rescue service does a good job, but of course we have no coastguard ships out in the deep sea. The hon. member also asked about lobsters on the Pacific coast, and whether I could reveal the deep secret of what had happened to them. Our department has tried at various times to transplant lobsters from the east coast to the west coast, but two things happen. On the west coast we have a fine crab fishery with big, aggressive crabs being the dominant population on the sea bottom. Lobsters have to moult their shells once a year, during which time they are soft and defenceless and undoubtedly this dominant population of crabs attacked and devoured them during this period.
The other reason is much simpler. Those hon. members who saw the film on lobsters last night will realize that in the early stage of their life the tiny lobsters float near the surface and become very widely scattered before dropping to the bottom to begin their adult life. We have never brought more than a few hundred lobsters at a time to the west coast, so the seed of these few lobsters becomes widely scattered by tides and currents. When they drop down to the bottom the density of population on the bottom is therefore very slight, since the lobsters are so widely dispersed. So it is most difficult for a male lobster to meet a female lobster in British Columbia waters and because of that we cannot get an increase of population out there. I think that covers all the points raised by hon. members.

Mr. Chairman, I would not like to have the minister leave a false impression by indicating that the Fraser river might be just a little wider than the length of this room. I am sure that hon. members will

Up where I happen to live the river is well over nine-tenths of a mile wide and I would say that this room might be one-fiftieth of a mile long.
The minister failed to answer three questions which I put to him which is the main reason for my rising at this time. I should like him to answer my first question. Have the Fraser river fishermen failed to conserve the fish during the past years and at the same time built up the fishing industry in British Columbia to the point where it is the greatest it has ever been this year?
Secondly, would he please tell the committee whether the fish which have spoiled came from gill net fishermen on the Fraser river or were they not fish caught out in the ocean and brought in by seine vessels to the packing houses?
Thirdly, what compensation if any does the Department of Fisheries intend to pay to those veterans who were settled in the upper reaches of the Fraser river above the Pattullo bridge with an undertaking by the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Veterans Affairs that they would be permitted to fish on that part of the river? That right is now being taken away under this section. I know the minister explained this before, and I gave my argument in one of my former speeches which I do not intend to repeat tonight. I shall not read again the letter which I received which quoted figures to support my argument.
